#4976. Bitcoin Lightning operators could recover stuck payments even after losing channel data

Core Lightning’s new recovery tool helps node operators reclaim funds from pending Bitcoin payments after losing channel data.

Core Lightning’s first 26.12 release candidate adds a way to reclaim funds from some pending Bitcoin Lightning payments.

It applies after an operator loses local channel data and a peer closes the channel by posting a transaction to Bitcoin. The tool gives the operator separate ways to reclaim outgoing funds or collect incoming funds, depending on the payment information that survived.

Core Lightning published the test build on Nov. 18, and still headed the project’s release list on Nov. 25 as a pre-release.

Bitcoin Optech covered the feature in its Nov. 20 newsletter and revisited it in its Nov. 24 podcast recap.

Core Lightning’s existing recovery process can reclaim the operator’s main channel balance when the peer posts a closing transaction the recovering node has never seen.

The change adds a new tool that addresses a separate output: the amount the closing transaction sets aside for a payment that was still pending.

Both recovery paths require a matching output in the closing transaction that remains unspent. For a payment the operator offered, the tool’s manual says the operator needs the payment hash and the expiry. Once the timelock expires, the operator can reclaim those funds.

For a payment the peer offered, the operator needs the preimage, the secret that matches the payment hash. The operator’s claim must be confirmed on Bitcoin before the peer reclaims the same output. Once the timelock expires, the peer can take the funds back.

The tool reconstructs the spending conditions for each payment the operator wants to recover and checks them against the closing transaction, and skips payments that are too small to have an output.

It produces signed transactions for the operator to review and broadcast manually.

Please enable JavaScript to verify and send this form.

Core Lightning 26.12rc1 tests recovery after an operator loses channel data and the peer force-closes the channel.

The tool handles pending-payment outputs. The main channel balance has its own recovery path.

The original node secret, channel and payment details, and the peer’s public commitment point are also required. Outputs that are absent or already spent cannot be recovered.

The two paths follow the tagged Core Lightning manual’s rules for payments offered by the operator or the closing peer.

The original node secret, channel and payment details, and the peer’s public commitment point are also required. Outputs that are absent or already spent cannot be recovered.

The operator needs the original node secret, the peer’s closing transaction, channel identifiers and key information, and details for each payment they want to recover.

A cooperating peer can supply the public commitment point tied to the closing transaction while keeping its private keys and commitment secrets private.

Core Lightning’s wallet recovery guide describes using the node secret and an emergency channel backup to reclaim the main balance after a peer closes the channel.

It also warns that restoring an outdated database can permanently lose funds, so recovering a pending payment depends on having enough information to reconstruct its particular output.

#4975. Australian Crypto Investors Turn to Loans Ahead of 2027 Tax Reform

Home » Crypto Market News » Australian Crypto Investors Turn to Loans Ahead of 2027 Tax Reform

Upcoming capital gains tax reforms are prompting crypto holders to reconsider how they access cash without selling their digital assets

One in five Australian cryptocurrency investors would consider borrowing against their digital assets rather than selling them, as upcoming tax changes push holders to rethink their financial strategies.

A survey commissioned by digital asset wealth platform Nexo found that 22.7% of Australian crypto holders would consider borrowing against their holdings instead of selling, compared with 10% of other investors.

The findings come as Australia prepares to overhaul its capital gains tax (CGT) system from July 1, 2027.

Nexo surveyed 1,000 Australian investors this October to examine how major expenses and rising living costs affect investment decisions.

The results suggest that crypto holders are more inclined to avoid selling their investments when they need additional funds.

Beyond the 22.7% considering borrowing, another 19.7% said they had delayed or decided against selling their crypto holdings.

Crypto investors can borrow against their existing holdings instead of selling them for cash. This allows them to access money while keeping their Bitcoin or other digital assets, and potentially benefit if their value increases.

The trend comes against a broader backdrop of financial pressure. According to the survey, 29.4% of all investors had delayed, reduced or cancelled a major purchase or financial plan over the previous 12 months.

The upcoming CGT reform is another factor investors may need to consider.

Under Australia’s current system, eligible individuals, trusts and partnerships can receive a 50% capital gains tax discount on assets held for more than 12 months.

From July 1, 2027, this discount will be replaced by cost base indexation and a 30% minimum tax on eligible gains.

Under transitional arrangements, gains accrued before that date will remain eligible for the existing 50% discount, while gains accumulated afterward will be subject to the new rules.

Crypto ownership in Australia is at a record high, with 2.79 million Australians holding or trading cryptocurrency, according to the figures cited in an Australian investor Study.

That equals about 24% of the country’s 11.5 million investors, up from roughly 15% in 2023, making crypto as widely held as exchange-traded funds (ETFs).

As ownership expands, the demand for financial products that allow investors to access liquidity without selling their holdings could also increase.

Consequently, as their holdings rise in value, more investors may look for ways to cover major expenses without selling their crypto.

The new CGT rules could make some investors think twice before selling crypto that has increased in value. As a result, more holders may consider borrowing against their holdings to cover major expenses without having to sell their assets and potentially trigger a capital gains tax bill.

#4973. $14.7B in ‘Lost’ Bitcoin Has Moved Since 2018: Report

$14.7B in ‘Lost’ Bitcoin Has Moved Since 2018: Report

Bitcoin that hasn't been moved in years is sometimes considered "lost" by industry onlookers, and one lawsuit is arguing that they've been "abandoned." But since 2018, roughly 10,000 supposedly lost Bitcoin wallets have sprung back to life.

Pseudonymous developer Quickben22 built a list in 2018 of 92,076 Bitcoin wallets that hadn't moved funds in more than six years, assuming the owners had lost their keys. Eight years later, the developer revisited the list to discover that 9,990 of those wallets have since moved a total of approximately 245,000 BTC, or just over $14.7 billion at Bitcoin's current price.

"Dormant is not the same as lost," Quickben22 told Decrypt. "I expected nearly all of the 92,076 addresses to still be silent after 8 years. About 89% are, but 9,990 have moved, and 14+ year old addresses are still waking up."

That distinction matters, as the findings come as a New York lawsuit brought by a pseudonymous plaintiff known as 'Noah Doe' tries to claim 39,069 dormant Bitcoin addresses as abandoned property, including wallets linked to Bitcoin creator Satoshi Nakamoto.

The plaintiffs argue the coins are "abandoned" under New York's lost property law. They say they found the wallets, reported them to the NYPD, and sent the owners notice by attaching on-chain messages to tiny Bitcoin transactions.

"It's like writing down the addresses of every locked house on a street, telling the police, and claiming whatever is inside because nobody answered the door," Quickben22 said.

Some wallets linked to the suit have since woken up, with several moving funds earlier this year—including one first funded in 2013 that shifted 411.45 BTC in October, then worth $33.4 million. One pseudonymous holder has also filed a motion to dismiss the case, claiming to still control a named wallet.

Quickben22's list was originally built for an app called Bitcoin Key Hunter, which guesses private keys at random and checks them against the dormant addresses in the hope of landing on one.

"It's like playing the lottery, but with much, much smaller odds," he said, before breaking down the math: roughly 1 in 10^43 across the whole list. "Those are about the odds of winning five Powerballs in a row," he added.

Quickben22 did not respond to Decrypt's query on whether he has successfully guessed the keys to any of the listed wallets.

It is impossible to know who exactly moved the funds from the supposedly lost wallets—it might not even be the original owner. An original owner tidying up old funds looks the same on-chain as someone who found a seed phrase in a drawer, or a hacker who got hold of a key that was never theirs.

"The blockchain shows that someone could sign, but not who," Quickben22 wrote.

Even when a wallet really is lost, the owner doesn't always let go.

Welshman James Howells has spent more than a decade trying to recover a hard drive holding around 8,000 BTC, which his then-girlfriend accidentally threw out during an office clear-out in 2013. He traced it to a landfill in Newport, Wales, and spent years seeking permission to dig it up, until a judge dismissed his case on environmental grounds. Howells called the ruling a "stitch-up."

Last year, he offered the local council £2.5 million to buy the landfill outright, Decrypt reported. The council didn't respond. He has since given up the search and is instead launching Ceiniog, a Bitcoin layer-2 network with a token he says is backed by the buried coins he can't access.

“MY view is this: As long as YOU (or anyone else in the world) can view the balance [and can] verify for yourself that it still contains 8,000 Bitcoin, then [the] Ceiniog coin is fully backed with its value,” he told Decrypt last year. “If those coins ever moved, Ceiniog instantly loses its backing and value. I am guaranteeing that those coins will never move—because the private key is on a [hard drive] in a landfill.”

Howells' 8,000 BTC haven't moved since 2013. On paper, they look exactly like the coins on Quickben22's list, and the kind the Noah Doe lawsuit wants declared abandoned.

#4972. Lido tightens Ethereum staking penalties as operators gain access to larger validators

Lido voters approved broader penalties to recover missed Ethereum staking rewards and other losses from operators’ collateral.

Lido voters backed a proposal on Nov. 23 to let the committee overseeing its two community staking modules recover more Ethereum staking losses from operators’ bonds.

In the March slashing case that prompted the vote, Lido’s contracts automatically recovered about 43% of the loss, while the operator voluntarily covered the rest.

The Snapshot result posted on Lido’s governance forum showed 53.8 million LDO in favor and 4.1 million against, enough to reach quorum. The off-chain vote backed a wider remit for the committee overseeing Lido’s two open-entry Community Staking Modules, 0x01 and 0x02.

The vote carried zero on-chain actions, so individual penalties must still be reported and settled separately.

The updated mandate extends an existing penalty mechanism used when operators divert block rewards. It would also cover staking rewards missed after slashing, along with incidents that could harm the protocol, such as withdrawal delays or risks to validator key security.

Committee members who backed the change called for documented evidence, credit for losses already recovered, and a chance for operators to respond.

Lido’s final incident report put the March 12 slashing at 0.7973122 ETH in penalties and missed rewards. When the six validators withdrew, Lido’s contracts automatically took 0.3459189 ETH from the operator’s bond to cover the withdrawal shortfall.

The operator voluntarily paid the remaining 0.4513933 ETH after the committee made contact, and Lido reported that the incident was fully resolved in April.

Lido published its final loss figures on April 22.

The amount Lido could collect at settlement would depend on the bond still available.

This graphic describes one resolved incident. Percentages are rounded.

Use Lido’s April 22 final accounting for the March 12 incident. Divide each reported amount by 0.7973122 ETH and round to the nearest whole percent for labels. Bar segment widths use the unrounded shares.

This graphic describes one resolved incident. Percentages are rounded.

In a similar case under the wider mandate, the committee could assess the missed rewards separately and lock collateral against that amount. The amount Lido could collect at settlement would depend on the bond left after the automatic deduction.

Please enable JavaScript to verify and send this form.

Under the penalty procedure, the report locks the assessed loss and any applicable fine, and the operator can compensate Lido or dispute the report. The committee can start an Easy Track motion to settle the penalty.

The locked collateral is burned when the motion is enacted, and Lido’s Easy Track rules give LDO holders at least 72 hours to object. Objections backed by at least 0.5% of total LDO supply stop the motion.

The bond backs all validators run under the same operator account in a module. Lido sizes the required collateral by the number of keys the operator runs.

In 0x01, a default operator posts 2.4 ETH for the first 32 ETH validator and 1.3 ETH for each additional key. The 0x02 module requires 32 ETH for the first key and 30 ETH for each additional key.

A 0x02 validator receives 32 ETH to start and can receive more stake after activation without increasing the required bond.

At the theoretical 2,048 ETH effective-balance ceiling, the 32 ETH first-key bond would equal about 1.56% of that balance. The 2.4 ETH first-key bond in 0x01 equals 7.5% of the validator’s 32 ETH balance.

Lido launched 0x02 on Oct. 23, and its October operator update reported nearly 800,000 ETH being validated in the established module. The first 30 keys in 0x02 had received seed deposits, or 960 ETH in all, with 54 more keys still queued at the time.

Kvorum’s record of a separate Nov. 18 motion shows the 0x02 allocation limit rose from 0.01% to 0.5% of Lido’s core pool. The higher limit lets the module take on more stake as deposits arrive.

Lido’s operator documentation says the collateral is held in stETH. If an assessed penalty exceeds the available bond, the excess becomes debt that can be recovered from future rewards or bond top-ups.

Queued keys that lose bond coverage stop receiving deposits, and unbonded validators can face exit requests. How much and how quickly the protocol can recover depends on what the operator has left in the bond and what comes in later.

#4971. French Senate Rejects Disclosure Rule for Crypto

French senators on Nov. 24 rejected a proposal that would have required taxpayers to disclose self-hosted cryptocurrency holdings exceeding €100,000.

They would have had to report those assets as of Dec. 31.

This would have been the case even if they had held the same coins since January without making any sales.

Two matching amendments to the French 2027 budget were rejected by the Senate during the first reading of the draft.

Senators Pascal Savoldelli and Anne-Sophie Romagny reintroduced the proposal after it briefly passed in the National Assembly earlier in the month.

French taxpayers must disclose their crypto assets held on foreign crypto platforms.

These amendments would have expanded disclosure requirements to wallets that owners directly control. This pertains to a wallet that is not managed by an exchange or another custodian.

The French National Assembly approved the €100,000 disclosure threshold in a 150-44 vote on Nov. 3. There were also eight abstentions.

The next day, the National Assembly voted down the entire revenue portion of the budget.

This vote brought down the wallet disclosure provision along with the rest of the budget.

However, the subsequent effort to revive the provision in the Senate was defeated.

It should be noted that the 2027 budget is still being considered at the time of writing.

The Senate also rejected two other crypto-related measures debated as part of the budget.

One was a provision to tax gains realized when holders exchange cryptocurrencies for certain stablecoins.

The second was a proposal to expand France's exit tax to include unrealized gains on cryptocurrencies held by taxpayers who move their tax residence outside the country.

#4970. Next Technology (NXTT) Sells 500 Bitcoin to Fund AI Push

Next Technology Holding (Nasdaq: NXTT) sold about 500 bitcoin last week and said it will put the money toward artificial intelligence projects, the latest public company to trim its bitcoin treasury as prices slide.

The Japan-based software firm disclosed in a filing with the Securities and Exchange Commission on Tuesday that it sold the coins on Nov. 21 for about $29.22 million. That works out to an average price of $58,468.11 per bitcoin, net of fees and expenses.

The sale leaves NXTT with 5,333 BTC. The company was paid in tether (USDT), the dollar-pegged stablecoin, rather than in dollars.

NXTT said it plans to use the proceeds for research and development of its AI-related initiatives, including its AI software products and services, as well as for general corporate purposes.

The sale is the first under a program the company’s board approved on Oct. 30. That program allows NXTT to sell or pledge its bitcoin “from time to time in one or more tranches,” through exchange sales, block trades or loans that use the coins as collateral, with the stated aim of “reducing risk exposure and enhancing liquidity.”

The filing also repeats a line from the company’s latest quarterly report that marks a clear break from its earlier approach. NXTT “does not currently expect to purchase additional Bitcoin,” the company said, adding that it has adjusted its strategy to focus on managing the coins it already holds.

The program has no expiration date and doesn’t require the company to sell any set amount. The board can change, pause or end it at any time. As of Nov. 24, NXTT said it had not pledged any of its bitcoin as collateral.

NXTT, which is incorporated in Wyoming but based in Saitama Prefecture, Japan, describes itself as running two strategies: AI-enabled software development and holding bitcoin. It keeps substantially all of its coins with Japan-based institutional custodians, according to its quarterly filing.

The company held 833 BTC at the end of 2024 and added 5,000 BTC in 2025, bringing its total to 5,833 BTC. Its filing puts the cost basis of those coins at about $183.1 million, or roughly $31,400 per bitcoin, meaning last week’s sale still came in well above what the company paid on average.

Falling prices have still hit the books. NXTT reported a net loss of $32.2 million for the first nine months of 2026, compared with net income of $295.1 million a year earlier. The company said the swing came mainly from a drop in the fair value of its digital assets.

The company has also been reshaping its leadership around AI. Earlier this month it named Chan Phang Chuen, a former platform architect focused on computing infrastructure and AI inference, as chief technical officer after Hongliang Liu resigned from the role.

NXTT joins a growing list of public companies selling bitcoin to fund other businesses. Ionic Digital sold 737 bitcoin this month to pay for a data center buildout, and Rumble sold two-thirds of its bitcoin as its AI cloud business delivered its first profitable quarter.

Miners have been selling too. Bitdeer sold all 281 bitcoin it mined last week and now holds none. Not every treasury company is stepping back, though. Strategy added 457 bitcoin for $29.6 million during the same week NXTT was selling.

Bitcoin has struggled to hold $60,000 this week amid heavy outflows from U.S. spot bitcoin ETFs, and NXTT sold its coins near those levels.

The company said the proceeds from any future sales or pledges will depend on market conditions and the timing of execution.

Jonah, co-host of the 1000x podcast, wrote on Nov. 24 to “get out while you still can” after crypto trader Ansem said his wallet had been hacked.

Jonah predicted that staying in crypto would carry a stigma. At 03:07 UTC on Nov. 25, trading app Bullpen said the known impact of its breach was limited to 19 early beta accounts.

At 03:53 UTC, Ansem advised users to withdraw their funds until he could confidently say they were safe.

Ansem’s initial post said he suspected that someone had accessed the Bullpen profile where he had imported the private key for a Solana wallet he used on Pump.fun, and Jonah’s quote-post came in response to that claim.

Bullpen’s first public notice came later Tuesday and identified Ansem as one of the users affected.

In its initial notice, Bullpen gave a preliminary range of 18 to 19 affected accounts, all opened between April and June 2024. The company said it took the affected test service offline.

Its Wednesday update gave a figure of 19 accounts and said it had seen no further movement of the funds at that point.

Bullpen said the attacker took over the older accounts, exposing wallets users had imported into them. For users who had imported a wallet, the access Bullpen described extended beyond the trading app to funds in that wallet.

The private key Ansem said he imported could authorize transfers from the wallet he used on Pump.fun. The company said 99.8% of the funds taken came from one account, which it did not name.

In a separate post early Wednesday, he distinguished between launching a token he considered worthless and selling it, which he said made someone a scammer.

Shiba Inu (SHIB) kept leaving crypto exchanges this week as the price of the meme cryptocurrency fell to levels last seen in the spring of 2021, and on Wednesday, the outflow picked up sharply.

According to CoinGlass data, 520.83 billion SHIB left exchanges over the past 24 hours. That amount made up most of the 757.51 billion SHIB that exchanges lost over the past seven days, and over the past 30 days, the outflow reached 2.88 trillion SHIB.

On Wednesday evening, SHIB was trading at $0.00000344, according to CoinGlass. So far this week, the token was down 4.78%, and its market capitalization went down to $2.02 billion, according to TradingView.

According to the weekly chart on TradingView, SHIB last traded at these levels in the spring of 2021, months before the token reached its all-time high of $0.00008845 on Oct. 28, 2021.

From early 2026 until mid-November, the price of SHIB held above $0.000004, and the yearly low stood at $0.00000411 at the July 17 close. In November, SHIB fell to $0.00000373, and in late November, the token dropped as low as $0.00000337. On Jan. 1, the token closed the day at $0.00000692, and since the start of the year, SHIB has lost 50.3% of its value, according to CoinGlass. As of Nov. 22, SHIB had lost 22.7% in November so far, according to CryptoRank.

The latest drop in SHIB came after Bitcoin fell back below $60,000 this week. On Saturday, Nov. 21, Bitcoin dropped as low as $55,150, its lowest price since September 2024. Over the past 24 hours, $57,590 worth of SHIB futures positions were liquidated, and $54,750 of that amount came from long positions on OKX, according to CoinGlass.

The Wednesday outflow was not the first large one this month. On Nov. 17, about 312 billion SHIB were withdrawn from exchanges, according to CryptoQuant. On the same day, the number of SHIB holders on Ethereum passed 1.7 million, according to Etherscan.

CoinGlass data also shows that since late 2024, the total SHIB balance on exchanges has gone down by 19.18 trillion tokens, or 20.54%, to 74.19 trillion, and over the same period, the price of SHIB fell by 88.39%. The remaining 74.19 trillion SHIB on exchanges make up 12.59% of the circulating supply and are worth about $254.75 million.

Most of the 24-hour outflow came from exchanges that CoinGlass groups as "Others," as their combined SHIB balance fell by 88.5% to 70.93 billion tokens. Over the same period, the SHIB balances of Binance and OKX barely changed, and Coinbase, Bitfinex and Bitstamp added SHIB.

As a result, in the week when the price of SHIB fell to levels last seen in 2021, exchanges lost more SHIB in a single day than over the previous six days combined, according to CoinGlass data.

#4966. GTA 6 PC Ports ‘Nuked’ Just Days Before Devs Expected It to Be Playable

GTA 6 PC Ports ‘Nuked’ Just Days Before Devs Expected It to Be Playable

Several major projects attempting to port Grand Theft Auto 6 to PC have been "nuked," according to community insiders. It comes as developers thought a playable port was just days away, after notorious Rockstar hacker Cyberleek released the game's files.

Both the Leonida GitHub page and the GTA6Modding Discord server—two of the most serious attempts at porting the latest Grand Theft Auto title to PC—have been removed. Other servers also involved in the AI-powered porting scene, such as the Chasm Server, have also locked down.

"Leonida and GTA6Modding have both been nuked," Freakman, a Chasm Server mod, wrote on Discord. "We have no affiliation with Cyberleek," they added. "Multiple servers have been struck, we're staying low for tonight."

Cyberleek released an Xbox build of GTA 6 on November 19, the day the game launched on consoles. However, they held back the main executable needed to run it and promised they'd release it if the CYBERLEEK meme coin hit a $15 million market cap.

Porting projects had been preparing for that file, expecting it'd be the key to making the port playable. The scene leans heavily on AI coding tools to speed up the reverse engineering needed to get console games running on PC, with developers describing themselves as "vibe coders."

The meme coin missed its $15 million target, but Cyberleek released the executable on Monday anyway. The next day, several GTA 6 porting projects were shut down.

"They're taking out servers left and right that are mentioning the leak," Chasm community member Weedgoose told Decrypt. "Some servers take the hit while others are going dark and are waiting for the flames to extinguish."

Some of the impacted community members have moved to alternative messaging platforms that are more private than Discord, Weedgoose said.

It appears the Leonida GitHub was removed by its creator, an apparent high school student, as it shows a 404 error page rather than a DMCA takedown page. That said, there's no way of knowing if the creator received a cease and desist (or similar correspondence) that led to this decision.

Chasm mod Freakman did not respond to Decrypt's request for comment regarding why the server has gone dark.

Take-Two Interactive, Rockstar's parent company, has been going after the leaks for months. In August, it filed subpoenas asking Discord and Microsoft, which owns GitHub, to hand over data that could help identify Cyberleek.

Rockstar has yet to announce an official PC version of GTA 6 yet. GamesBeat reported in October that one could arrive in Q1 of 2027—and the prospect of an unofficial port releasing in advance of that would likely dent sales.

Rockstar did not respond to Decrypt's request for comment.

#4965. Ukraine Legalizes Crypto After One-Day Delay

Home » Regulations » Ukraine Legalizes Crypto After One-Day Delay

Crypto-embracing Bill No. 10225-d gets the highest-priority treatment following a slight procedural delay.

Ukraine’s parliament has approved a bill to bring cryptocurrency trading, custody and taxation under a formal legal framework.

The measure, Bill No. 10225-d, passed after lawmakers postponed consideration a day earlier, a pause that had raised questions about its immediate path despite renewed support from the parliamentary finance committee for the revised text.

The Ukraine crypto bill is designed to legalize and regulate the domestic virtual-asset market rather than leave it in a largely undefined legal space.

Its scope includes tax treatment for crypto activity as well as rules for trading platforms and custodial services.

That approach would place businesses handling customer assets under a clearer licensing and compliance structure.

BREAKING: Ukraine officially passes law to LEGALIZE crypto, effective July 1, 2027. pic.twitter.com/6KxnNa7N2b

The framework comes into practice on July 1, 2027. It offers more certainty over how digital-asset transactions are treated by authorities, though implementation details will matter as much as the legislation itself.

Ukraine has maintained an active crypto sector despite the strains of war, with digital assets playing a visible role in fundraising and cross-border transfers.

Formalizing the market has therefore carried significance beyond ordinary financial regulation: it could help define how crypto businesses operate in an economy still managing exceptional pressures with the fifth year of war with Russia coming along.

The Ukraine crypto bill’s journey shows how quickly crypto policy can shift even when lawmakers broadly support regulation.

BREAKING: Zelensky President of Ukraine officially legalizes Bitcoin & crypto after parliament passes the bill with 271 vote pic.twitter.com/qt9C7jcNVK

The November 24, 2026 postponement followed committee backing for a revised version, while the subsequent passage points to a resolution of at least some of those immediate obstacles.

Questions remain over the final tax mechanics, the timing of licensing requirements and which agencies will oversee different parts of the sector. Market participants will also watch for secondary rules that determine the practical burden on exchanges, brokers and wallet providers.

Ukraine’s crypto move matters because it adds another sizable European market pursuing rules for digital assets rather than relying on prohibition or legal ambiguity.

The Ukraine crypto legislation may give local firms a route toward greater legitimacy, but the ultimate test will be whether the resulting framework is workable enough to retain innovation while improving crypto oversight.

#4964. CleanSpark Weighs Selling More Bitcoin Than It Mines After $987M Loss

CleanSpark (Nasdaq: CLSK) may sell more bitcoin than it mines as it works to lower risk on its balance sheet, President and CFO Gary Vecchiarelli said Tuesday, after the miner posted a $987.1 million net loss for its fiscal year ended Sept. 30, as lower bitcoin prices hit the value of its holdings.

“We see the selling of a small amount of bitcoin in excess of the quarterly production to be one way of derisking,” Vecchiarelli said on the company’s earnings call. He added that CleanSpark will be “very reactionary to markets” and use that cash to avoid dilution or new debt.

Vecchiarelli said CleanSpark already aims to sell virtually all of the bitcoin it mines to run the business, and that it has sold some bitcoin since year-end to build cash for acquisitions it expects to make soon. “It is reasonable to expect that we will fund highly accretive acquisitions and development of projects by selling or borrowing against our bitcoin,” he said.

The Las Vegas-based company reported full-year revenue of $576.5 million, down 25%. The loss came to $3.74 per basic share, and adjusted EBITDA was a loss of $304.2 million. Vecchiarelli said about two-thirds of the swing from last year’s $364 million profit came from noncash mark-to-market losses on bitcoin.

CleanSpark recorded a $281.6 million loss on the fair value of its bitcoin for the year, versus a $425.6 million gain a year earlier. It also took $177.1 million in impairment charges, mostly tied to turning its Sandersville, Georgia, mining site into a data center. Bitcoin ended the fiscal year near $83,600, down from about $114,000, the CFO said.

The fourth quarter looked different. CleanSpark earned $9.8 million, or 4 cents a share, helped by a $305.6 million gain on its bitcoin, even as revenue dropped 46% from a year earlier to $120.9 million. Analysts had expected a loss of 33 cents a share and revenue of about $134.3 million, Investing.com reported.

The miner produced 7,253 BTC during the year, down 8% as network difficulty rose and it curtailed some machines, and ended September with about 200,000 machines running, down from 225,000 at the end of June. That cut lifted fleet efficiency to 14.8 joules per terahash, while average hashrate fell to 36.0 EH/s.

CleanSpark held 13,530 BTC, including pledged collateral, at the end of September, worth about $1.1 billion then. #4962. Morning Minute: Jensen Returns, Markets Soar (Except Crypto)

Morning Minute: Jensen Returns, Markets Soar (Except Crypto)

Morning Minute is a daily newsletter written by Tyler Warner. The analysis and opinions expressed are his own and do not necessarily reflect those of Decrypt. And check out our daily news show 'FOMO HOUR' covering all of the top stories and market action.

Six days after Nvidia’s board chair told investors “the Nvidia board does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO,” the board voted unanimously to reinstate him as president, CEO and director, effective immediately.

Nvidia shares rose 33% to around $167, adding roughly a trillion dollars of market value in a session. Huang’s personal net worth climbed about $36.6 billion on his 3.5% stake, moving him to 13th on the Forbes global list. Short sellers took roughly $12.2 billion in paper losses, their worst single day since at least 2019, which wiped out the $10.5 billion they had booked the prior week.

The stock market absolutely ripped on the news. The Nasdaq closed up 6.51% at 24,089, its best day since April 2025. The S&P gained 4.7%, the Dow was +3%, and the VIX collapsed 25.8% to 26.62.

Bitcoin went along with the ride—for a few hours. It touched $63,929 intraday, up 5.1%, then spent the afternoon handing it back and finished near $61,000, barely up on the day. The ETFs used the pump to exit more, with BTC ETFs seeing another $570M in outflows on the day.

ETH and other majors also closed red. Alts gave back their gains. And the CMC top 20 index managed just 0.20% gain.

That’s a 19 to 1 ratio between what the Nasdaq captured and what Bitcoin kept, on the same catalyst, on the same day. Pain for the crypto bulls.

What makes it even more painful, is that crypto fell with AI stocks the whole way down, and the standard explanation was that both trade on the same liquidity and the same risk appetite. Monday tested that and the correlation fell through. The AI trade got a catalyst and markets bounced. Crypto didn’t bounce with it.

As for Nvidia’s reversal decision itself, questions remain to say the least. The board says it was satisfied with Huang’s “candor and ability to lead,” and that input from senior U.S. officials left it confident his return “poses no national security risk.” Trump publicly pushed for it and said the board had sought assurance on the espionage allegations. What actually changed between November 17 and November 23 hasn’t been explained. The independent directors’ investigation is still open, and Nvidia is now standing up a board committee for national security and export-control oversight plus recruiting a chief compliance officer.

Perhaps answers will trickle out over time. The AI trade may not need them anyway. And crypto, well, it's in its own world right now, waiting for its own catalysts (likely quantum-related). But it’s very unclear that catalyst is coming in 2026, and it’s becoming clear that many are not interested in waiting for the answers…

#4960. CertiK Trains Interpol Investigators to Trace and Freeze Stolen Crypto

CertiK Trains Interpol Investigators to Trace and Freeze Stolen Crypto

Blockchain security firm CertiK trained police investigators from across Asia and the South Pacific in tracing stolen crypto and securing asset freezes at an INTERPOL meeting in Hanoi, the company said.

The 3rd INTERPOL Asia and South Pacific Working Group Meeting on Cybercrime ran from October 27 to October 30, 2026. It was organized by INTERPOL's Cybercrime Directorate and Vietnam's Ministry of Public Security. CertiK said senior law enforcement officials from 20 countries attended, with stablecoin issuer Tether and South Korean exchange Upbit among the other private-sector partners.

CertiK's sessions focused on the two stages of recovering stolen crypto: mapping how funds move after a theft, then using that evidence to ask exchanges to freeze them.

Officers worked through a real wallet-compromise case, using open-source block explorers and CertiK's compliance software to follow stolen funds through token swaps, cross-chain bridges and intermediary wallets to three deposit addresses at an exchange. The exercise included spotting address-poisoning decoys, which attackers use to send investigators down false trails.

CertiK's team then explained the process for contacting the exchange, using its law enforcement portal and filing formal requests to freeze the funds.

Other sessions covered how to read wallet activity before and after a suspicious transaction, how smart contract vulnerabilities and audit findings can inform an investigation, and how to tell apart attacks involving compromised signing keys, phishing and social engineering.

"Investigators need both a clear picture of how an attack happened and a practical route to act on the evidence," Esme Pau, CertiK's head of capital markets and policy, said in a statement.

Fellow security firm Group-IB, which also presented, tweeted that the four-day meeting drew more than 80 participants from over 43 countries and regions. INTERPOL's working group for heads of regional cybercrime units first met in Manila in September 2024.

The training comes as INTERPOL steps up its work on crypto-enabled crime. In July 2026, it said that a 20-year-old Thai suspect's wallet had moved more than $122.5 million in romance-scam proceeds in 10 months, using cross-chain swaps to hide the trail. The case was one of many in Operation First Light, a 97-country sweep that led to 5,811 arrests.

💫 Group-IB participated in the 3rd @INTERPOL_Cyber Asia & South Pacific Cybercrime Working Group Meeting in Hanoi, Vietnam, held from 27–30 October 2026. Led by INTERPOL’s Cybercrime Directorate - Asia & South Pacific Cybercrime Operations Desk and co-hosted by Vietnam’s… pic.twitter.com/tYaKEUnaXL

— Group-IB Global (@GroupIB) November 3, 2026

In October 2026, Operation Serengeti III recovered more than $105 million across 21 African countries and shut two illegal crypto mining centers in Angola. It followed Operation Catalyst, in which INTERPOL and Afripol arrested 83 people in 2025. INTERPOL's member countries also designated scam-compound networks, which channel billions of dollars through crypto, a transnational criminal threat in November 2025.

Tether, which can freeze USDT at flagged addresses, has become a regular partner in such investigations. In April 2026, it froze more than $344 million in USDT across two Tron addresses in coordination with U.S. authorities. Earlier this month, it formed a task force with Tron and Chainalysis to trace illicit USDT on Tron and help police freeze it.

Stablecoins such as USDT remain a concern for investigators. Earlier this month, a UK taskforce convened by think tank RUSI warned that USDT has been linked to Russian-speaking laundering networks, citing a July 2025 HM Treasury report.

Pau cited about $2.6 billion in Web3 security losses during the first three quarters of 2026, with compromised keys, targeted phishing and supply-chain attacks among the main causes.

CertiK's H1 2026 report recorded some $1.32 billion lost across 344 incidents, and its security dashboard puts third-quarter losses at $1.28 billion.

That figure predates the largest theft of the year. The FBI has attributed October's $6.4 billion hack of Binance, which took place during the Hanoi meeting, to North Korea's TraderTraitor group. North Korea has denied involvement.

#4959. Bitcoin ‘As Important as It’s Ever Been’ if Inflation Rises, Coinbase CEO Says

"Bitcoin investors tend to sell BTC when there's a big IPO. Then they come back."

That's Coinbase CEO Brian Armstrong's take on Bitcoin investor behavior, less than a week after the record-breaking $93.5 billion IPO of Claude creator Anthropic.

"Historically, people rotate out of it to take advantage of a big IPO. Then they come back in," Armstrong wrote on X earlier today.

The limited window of opportunity to invest in an IPO helps explain the behavior Armstrong described. For an investor to buy at the IPO price, there's only a certain period during which they can request an allocation of shares. After that, the price is determined by the market.

On Nov. 19, Anthropic went public on the Nasdaq, and that brief window of opportunity mattered.

Shares were priced at $83, up from the $70-$78 range indicated just two days earlier. Anthropic's stock, trading under the ticker ANT, opened at $111.50.

If you bought at that opening price, you paid about 34% more per share than an investor who received an allocation at the IPO price.

When the IPO closed on Nov. 20, 1.127 billion shares had been sold, including 147 million additional shares purchased by underwriters exercising their option.

Of the $93.5 billion in gross proceeds, Anthropic itself received around $91.6 billion. The rest went to existing shareholders.

There was also a separate $26 billion private placement involving investors such as Microsoft, Nvidia, Google and others. In total, the combined transactions were valued at $119.5 billion.

As for the longer-term case for holding BTC, Armstrong's point concerns investors' expectations about the future purchasing power of their money.

"If you think there is going to be more inflation and money printing in the future, bitcoin is as important as ever."

At the heart of the matter is Bitcoin's 21 million supply limit.

If you expect governments to continue expanding the money supply, you may still be excited by the prospect of a major IPO. And you may sell some of your BTC to participate in it.

Armstrong's argument is that the window of opportunity to participate in a major IPO eventually closes.

However, the reasons investors bought Bitcoin in the first place may remain long after the newly listed stock starts trading.

#4958. HRF Announces Funding of Seven Bitcoin Projects for People Living Under Authoritarian Regimes

Together, these efforts help human rights defenders, journalists, nonprofits, and individuals hold, send, and verify their money freely under repression.

HRF’s grantees for Round III of 2026 are:

Many people want to self-custody bitcoin, but in much of the world, buying a hardware wallet is too expensive. CryoBrick transforms feature phones into offline Bitcoin signing devices. Because it looks and works like an ordinary phone, activists living under authoritarian regimes can self-custody bitcoin while maintaining plausible deniability. Technical Director Apalok will use HRF’s support to conduct comprehensive security hardening and peer review, integrate Bitchat for offline messaging, and publish how-to guides, expanding access to bitcoin and the property rights it protects to a far larger global user base.

Bitcoin’s benefits remain out of reach for many African communities because high-quality education resources do not exist in their local languages. Exonumia, an open-source project that translates Bitcoin educational content, is building a Bitcoin Glossary in 21 African languages. The project will coordinate a continent-wide community of translators through three in-person and 12 virtual translation sprints, where native speakers review and validate more than 250 terms. Because every term is validated by native speakers rather than machines, the approved terms give wallet developers a trustworthy foundation for localizing bitcoin software into African languages, extending access to bitcoin education and the financial freedom it offers. HRF’s support will see the glossary published as a free public resource.

In much of Africa, democratic elections remain a struggle and most countries are not fully free. Exacerbating this, evidence of fraud documented by citizens is often lost because paper forms go missing and photos and messages cannot be verified. Pawavox, created by Nigerian civic-tech founder Jason Omu, is a platform that gives election observers and human rights defenders a new way to record irregularities. Using Pawavox, observers capture short video or voice reports, each GPS-tagged and timestamped. This evidence is then published to Nostr, a decentralized communications protocol, as a record that is much harder for anyone to tamper with. HRF’s grant will help fund the completion of the Nostr integration and expansion across Africa, helping protect the integrity of the evidence on which democratic accountability depends.

Branded hardware wallets are a common way to self-custody bitcoin, but under repressive regimes, they can be expensive and attract unwanted attention. SeedSigner is an open-source signing device that users assemble themselves from inexpensive, widely available parts, so there is no finished-device supply chain for an attacker to compromise. It currently runs on a small computer, called a Raspberry Pi Zero, which can be unavailable in regions that need self-custody most. Lead maintainer Keith Mukai will use HRF’s support to migrate the SeedSigner code to more widely available hardware, ending dependence on any single manufacturer. Then, more individuals under repressive regimes will be able to hold their own bitcoin without trusting anyone else.

Nigeria is one of the world’s most active digital asset markets, but the legal path to acquiring bitcoin runs through exchanges that collect troves of identity and transactional data. At the same time, many rural Nigerian homes are receiving solar electricity for the first time, but much of that power goes unused in the daytime. Strandedwatt, a bitcoin mining initiative, installs small open-source Bitcoin miners in homes, converting surplus solar power into bitcoin, which is paid privately and directly to host households. The next step, backed by HRF, will see Bitnob CEO and project lead Bernard Parah deploy 100 Jua Kali miners in these homes and publish an open-source playbook other communities can replicate. Meanwhile, households excluded by the Nigerian financial system gain a permissionless path to freedom money.

A commercial Bitcoin hardware wallet has software and hardware the user cannot inspect, and carrying one can signal to outsiders that someone owns bitcoin. Specter DIY is a fully open-source, air-gapped Bitcoin hardware wallet that anyone can build from off-the-shelf components and verify line by line. There is no purchase record, and the finished device does not look like a Bitcoin wallet at all. For activists in Belarus, dissidents in Venezuela, and journalists in Burma, it is a path to financial self-sovereignty. HRF’s grant to the Specter Association, the nonprofit that maintains the project, helps fund hardware costs, AI tooling, and vulnerability bounties, ensuring the developers behind a self-custody tool dissidents can inspect and verify remain supported.

#4956. Justice Department Moves to Forfeit $1.1B in USDC From North Korea's Binance Hack

Justice Department Moves to Forfeit $1.1B in USDC From North Korea's Binance Hack

The U.S. Justice Department has moved to permanently take control of more than $1.1 billion in crypto stolen by North Korean hackers in the record $6.4 billion theft from Binance.

The department filed a civil forfeiture claim on Monday for the funds, which are held in USDC, the stablecoin issued by Circle, it said. The assets were already subject to a restraining order the government had requested after the hack, and Circle provided "valuable assistance," the department said.

The filing is part of a wider U.S. effort to help Binance recover the stolen funds. Since the October 29 hack, the U.S. has helped freeze, seize or return more than $2.9 billion in crypto, according to the department. That is up from the $2.7 billion in frozen assets it reported on November 12, when it said it had court approval to seize or restrain more than $1.2 billion.

"Swift coordination between the government and private sector partners helped prevent a substantial portion of those assets from disappearing," Assistant Attorney General A. Tysen Duva of the department's Criminal Division said in a statement.

Secret Service investigators identified and froze stolen funds "within minutes of the hack," said Todd Bratz, special agent in charge of the agency's Criminal Investigations Division. The Secret Service is investigating the case alongside the FBI and IRS Criminal Investigation.

The FBI has attributed the theft to TraderTraitor, which the Justice Department describes as members of the North Korean military. North Korea has denied involvement, and Binance has set aside $6.34 billion to cover customer losses.

Stablecoin issuers Tether and Circle froze funds after the hack. But the hackers have kept moving what they still control. After two weeks of inactivity, wallets tied to the hack began moving Ethereum in mid-November.

At least $247 million has since been funneled through Bitcoin coinjoins, a mixing technique that pools funds to obscure their origin, blockchain analytics firm Elliptic said on Monday. Elliptic estimates that about $2.85 billion has been frozen and that roughly $2.35 billion remains in addresses tied to the theft.

Binance has also pursued the funds through the courts, winning a $6.5 billion freezing order from Abu Dhabi courts that can be served on wallet holders via the blockchain.

#4955. CZ Urges 1Password Users to Change All Their Passwords

After a hacker stole customer data, Binance founder Changpeng Zhao advised 1Password users to change all the passwords stored in the service.

1Password offered different advice about what users should do after the incident was disclosed on Nov. 25. The password management service said hackers hadn't gained access to the passwords stored in users' vaults, so there was no need to reset them.

"If you use 1Password, recommend you to change ALL your passwords. It's a pain in the neck, but necessary," Zhao said on X, replying to a post from Coin Bureau about the breach.

If you have a crypto exchange login stored in 1Password, this distinction is important.

1Password says hackers could access the email address a customer uses to log in to the service. But they couldn't see the exchange password saved in the customer's vault.

Scammers could still use the stolen email addresses to contact people they know are 1Password users.

1Password started investigating on Nov. 19 after detecting signs of possible unauthorized access to an employee's corporate GitHub account.

From there, the hacker was able to steal private source code and inject malicious code into 1Password's backend services. The malicious code then downloaded certain administrative data about customers.

1Password publicly disclosed the breach on Nov. 25, six days later.

The company did not specify how many customers were affected or explain exactly how the hacker managed to take over the employee's account.

The stolen data included customer names, login email addresses, account and user IDs, and timestamps indicating account creation and last use.

The hacker also gained access to 1Password's software development and deployment systems.

1Password disabled the compromised employee's GitHub account and revoked the stolen access token.

The company also restored a clean version of the affected service and revoked or replaced potentially exposed internal credentials.

1Password also engaged independent security experts to review its response.

1Password recommends that customers check the 1Password app or type the company's website address directly into their browser if they receive an unexpected invitation or recovery message.

The company says it will never contact users to request their account password or Secret Key.

Update: 1Password claims that there is no need to change one's 1Password account password or any of the passwords saved in one's vault. No customer passwords were exposed in this incident.

Hi CZ! There’s no need to change your 1Password account password or any of the passwords you’ve saved in your vault. No customer passwords were exposed in this incident. We don’t store your account password or Secret Key, and getting into our backend systems didn’t give the attacker the keys to decrypt your vault. The attacker did copy account information for some customers, including names and email addresses, so we recommend watching for 1Password invitations or account recovery emails you weren’t expecting. The department announced the results of an anti-scam surge that followed President Donald Trump’s Executive Order 14390, signed March 6. Since then, prosecutors have acted in more than 400 cases, bringing new charges, extraditions, guilty verdicts and sentences across 85 federal districts.

U.S. agents also helped police in more than 10 countries raid foreign scam call centers and compounds that targeted Americans. Thirty defendants were extradited to face charges in U.S. courts.

“Predatory scams against the American people will not be tolerated,” Attorney General Todd Blanche said. “The unprecedented results of this surge are just the beginning.”

Crypto sits at the center of much of the effort. The State Department said the U.S. and Southeast Asian law enforcement it funds and trains have helped freeze more than $1 billion in stolen cryptocurrency and take down more than 1.4 million fraudulent websites and accounts.

The Justice Department’s Scam Center Strike Force, formed in 2025 to go after Southeast Asian crypto fraud, says its crypto seizure team has restrained about $1.08 billion in cryptocurrency from these schemes. The team is focused on returning stolen funds to victims.

The FBI’s Operation Blackout has restrained nearly $17 billion in illicit funds, seized more than 14,000 digital devices and helped dismantle more than 29 scam compounds across Asia, Africa and the Middle East, the department said. The FBI also helped free and repatriate more than 2,200 trafficked workers forced to run scams inside those compounds.

“The message to these scam syndicates is clear: if you target Americans, justice will find you,” FBI Director Kash Patel said.

In the past month alone, the Criminal Division filed or unsealed charges against more than 30 scam defendants, including those tied to Southeast Asian scam centers running crypto investment fraud schemes. Other cases involved inheritance fraud, jury duty imposters working from Georgia prisons and sweepstakes schemes aimed at elderly Americans.

The Secret Service said it has restrained more than $200 million in illicit funds during the surge. One of its cases identified a crypto investment conspiracy run from scam centers in Cambodia that targeted at least 174 U.S. victims. In October, a Chinese national was extradited from the Netherlands and arraigned in California over his alleged role.

In Moldova, State Department-backed raids in October shut down five call centers and led to the detention of eight suspected coordinators who allegedly ran fake crypto trading platforms. The SEC said that in the last year it charged three purported crypto asset trading platforms and four investment clubs with defrauding retail investors of more than $14 million.

Homeland Security Investigations said its fraud cases have led to the seizure or freezing of more than $120 million, including funds held in bank and cryptocurrency accounts.

The crackdown builds on months of pressure on overseas fraud rings. Trump planned to highlight the push against overseas crypto scams in October, and the U.S. government seized more than $580 million in crypto linked to Southeast Asian scam networks in February. In October 2025, prosecutors moved to seize 127,271 bitcoin tied to a Southeast Asian scam operation.

The stakes are large. Citing Gallup, the department said 10% of U.S. adults experienced a scam last year, directly or through someone in their household, and Americans lost an estimated $68 billion to scams in 2025, including crypto investment scams.

The department noted that an indictment is merely an allegation and that all defendants are presumed innocent until proven guilty.

Eligible professional investors can use USDC to buy exposure to a Japanese dividend stock fund through Hong Kong’s HashKey Earn. To exit, they submit a redemption request, and HashKey expects settlement on T+5 under the issuer’s dealing calendar and settlement arrangements.

SBI Holdings, Sumitomo Mitsui Financial Group and the Solana Foundation said they completed agreements for a new joint-venture structure and that the former SBI R3 Japan began operating under its new name.

The partners plan to use Solana to distribute Japanese assets and develop services in stablecoin payments, financial and real-world asset tokenization, and on-chain asset management.

The partners intend to start with practical uses in Japan before expanding across Asia and linking up with global markets.

DigiFT and SBI Global Asset Management announced the token JX on July 15. DigiFT issued the token on Solana as a depositary receipt linked to the SBI Japan High Dividend Equity Fund’s growth type, managed by SBI Asset Management.

The fund invests mainly in listed Japanese companies and seeks returns from dividends and rising share prices. DigiFT says the growth structure makes no distributions at either the fund or token level.

Qualified investors first gained access through Singapore-based DigiFT on July 14, according to SBI Global Asset Management. On Nov. 5, SBI Global Asset Management announced a second distribution channel through HashKey Earn, a service of the licensed Hong Kong platform HashKey Exchange.

That gave eligible investors a second place to buy JX while SBI Asset Management continued to run the underlying portfolio.

#4952. Europol Traces $28M in Crypto Behind Europe's Illegal Streaming Industry

Europol Traces $28M in Crypto Behind Europe's Illegal Streaming Industry

Law enforcement agencies from 11 countries have traced more than €26 million ($28 million) in crypto payments linked to illegal TV streaming services, in an operation that brought in crypto exchanges Binance and Coinbase and blockchain analytics firm Chainalysis, Europol said on Tuesday.

The five-day operation, held at the Spanish National Police headquarters in Seville from November 16 to November 20, 2026, disrupted 57 illegal IPTV services. Investigators also identified 321 websites illegally offering copyrighted content, which together receive more than 7.3 million visits a year. Analysis of the crypto transactions is continuing.

Investigators are increasingly targeting the money behind illegal streaming services, not just the services themselves.

Last week, Chainalysis joined Europol, law enforcement from 11 countries, and industry partners including Binance and Coinbase in Seville for a five-day… pic.twitter.com/XqV0Hima26

— Chainalysis (@chainalysis) November 24, 2026

IPTV, or internet protocol television, services sell access to television channels, live sports and films over the internet. Illegal providers charge a few euros a month for unauthorized access to premium content, often taking subscription payments in crypto, according to Europol.

During the operation, investigators traced suspicious transactions across blockchains to find links between illegal services, the crypto wallets receiving payments and the people controlling them.

Europol said the operation reflected a shift in strategy. Rather than focusing only on shutting down streaming services, investigators are increasingly targeting the financial infrastructure behind them, because taking a service offline does not necessarily stop the people running it.

Europol has gone after criminals' crypto in other cases, too. In June 2026, its Operation Endgame froze more than €41 million ($47 million) in crypto linked to infostealer malware, and in March it helped disrupt a proxy network whose payment platform had received more than $5.7 million in crypto.

Around 40 people took part, including 30 law enforcement officers from Belgium, Bulgaria, Croatia, Greece, Ireland, Italy, the Netherlands, Portugal, Romania, Spain and the U.S.

Europol coordinated the operation through its Intellectual Property Crime Coordinated Coalition, a unit supported by the European Union Intellectual Property Office (EUIPO), which also took part alongside INTERPOL and the Audio-visual Anti-Piracy Alliance (AAPA). The information gathered will feed into national investigations to identify suspects and trace assets.

An estimated 60 million people in Europe use unauthorized IPTV services, costing legitimate providers €4.83 billion ($5.3 billion) a year and governments a further €1.08 billion ($1.2 billion) in lost taxes, according to AAPA figures cited by Europol. Demand appears to be growing: visits to websites offering sign-ups for illegal IPTV services rose 10% in 2023, an EUIPO study found.

Europol ran a similar operation last year. In November 2025, a week-long cyber-patrol in Alicante, Spain, traced about $55 million in crypto linked to piracy services and referred 25 illegal IPTV services to crypto providers for disruption, The Record reported at the time.

Crypto also features in older piracy cases. In Germany, the alleged operator of defunct piracy site Movie2K has been offered a deal to end his money laundering and tax evasion trial if he hands over 40,000 BTC. Prosecutors believe he still holds about 56,000 BTC, bought with proceeds from the site before it shut down in 2013.

The offer came days after German lawmakers approved new powers allowing customs officials to seize crypto and other assets of unclear origin without first opening a criminal case.

#4951. Bithumb Says October Hack Exposed Passports, Bank Accounts and Wallet Addresses

South Korean crypto exchange Bithumb said Wednesday that an October hack of its internal systems exposed more people and far more personal data than it first disclosed, including passport numbers, bank account numbers and crypto wallet addresses.

The exchange also said the intruder had access for about 15 days before being shut out, not the roughly one hour it reported last month.

In an updated notice posted Nov. 25, Bithumb said a follow-up review of the breach of Daou Office, its internal mobile groupware system, turned up additional affected people and additional types of data. The company said the new findings stem from the same incident it disclosed on Oct. 29.

Bithumb now says an unauthorized outside party accessed the groupware system from 1:49 p.m. on Oct. 12 to 3:22 p.m. on Oct. 27, Korea time, and took personal information and files stored there.

That is a sharp change from its first account. Bithumb had said the hack lasted about an hour, from 11:28 a.m. to 12:27 p.m. on Oct. 27, and that it detected the intrusion at 12:14 p.m. that day. The revised timeline means the attacker went unnoticed for more than two weeks.

Bithumb first reported that the data of 6,444 customers and 715 employees, or 7,159 people in total, had been exposed. It did not give an updated count on Wednesday. The notice lists customers, employees of partner companies and current and former staff among those affected.

The list of exposed data now runs to 19 items. It includes member numbers, names, mobile numbers, email addresses, dates of birth, resident registration numbers, passport numbers and driver’s license numbers.

It also covers bank account numbers, home addresses, gender, nationality, copies of ID documents, occupations, employer names and work contact details, as well as transaction histories and wallet addresses. Bithumb said not every item applies to every person, and that affected users will be told individually by email and text message what was taken.

For crypto users, the wallet addresses and transaction records stand out. Paired with names and phone numbers, that kind of data can help scammers target people they know hold digital assets.

Bithumb said Daou Office is an internal business system separate from customer exchange accounts and asset data. It said it has found no sign that its exchange service systems or customer database were directly breached, and that it has stepped up real-time monitoring of unusual trades and withdrawals.

The exchange said it blocked the attacker’s IP addresses, fixed the vulnerability behind the incident and is running a security review of all of its externally exposed services. It has also set up a dedicated support desk for victims that covers financial and legal counseling as well as compensation reviews.

“We will take responsibility for all harm confirmed to have resulted from this personal information breach and provide all necessary support and compensation to affected customers,” Bithumb said.

Bithumb warned users that it never asks for passwords, verification codes or OTP details by phone, text or messenger. It urged anyone who gets such a request to stop responding, confirm through its official app or customer center and report any financial losses to police.

The disclosure adds to a difficult year for the exchange. Bithumb mistakenly credited users with billions of dollars in bitcoin in February, and regulators fined it $24 million and imposed a six-month partial suspension in March over anti-money laundering violations.

It also comes as South Korea weighs new rules for crypto exchanges, including a 20% cap on ownership stakes. Brokerages including Mirae Asset Securities and Daishin Securities have also suffered a series of cyberattacks.

“We are thoroughly investigating the cause of the incident,” Bithumb said.

#4950. South Korea wants banks to own more than 50% of domestic stablecoin issuers

South Korea’s stablecoin proposal gives banks majority control and establishes reserve-backed redemption protections for holders.

South Korea’s financial regulator proposed limiting initial domestic stablecoin issuance to licensed groups in which banks collectively own more than 50%.

Under the plan, a fintech or technology company could still hold the largest individual stake, as the Financial Services Commission (FSC) outlined on Nov. 24.

The legislative proposal calls stablecoins digital payment tokens and defines them as assets pegged to one currency and used mainly for payments. Issuers would put the tokens into circulation at an equivalent value in the underlying currency and would be barred from paying holders interest.

A domestic issuer would need an FSC license and at least 5 billion won in equity capital. Applicants would have to show they have the staff and facilities to operate, submit a viable business plan, and explain how they would prevent conflicts of interest.

Major shareholders and executives would also have to meet eligibility requirements.

The issuer would also need FSC approval for its issuance plan, including how many tokens it intended to issue, the maximum it could issue, how it would manage reserves, and how holders could redeem their tokens.

When a holder asked to redeem, the issuer would have to pay the equivalent value in currency without delay.

To meet those requests, issuers would keep reserves worth at least 100% of outstanding issuance with a reserve manager such as a bank. The proposal would shield the reserves from third-party seizure or setoff.

Under the proposed redemption rules, the institution managing the reserves could pay holders directly if the issuer went bankrupt, lost its license, or could no longer handle normal issuance and redemption after a disruption such as a hack.

The FSC says holders would have priority when the reserve manager makes those payments.

Platforms could only list tokens with the applicable approval or filing. The same requirement would apply to digital asset firms that trade, broker, or hold those tokens in custody.

The FSC said it would support deliberations in the National Assembly, while a later presidential decree would set detailed shareholder rules for domestic stablecoin issuers.

Ansem Meme Coin Crashes After $2.57 Million Wallet Drain, Bullpen Confirms Security Breach

Crypto trading platform Bullpen confirmed a security incident on Tuesday after a wallet belonging to popular crypto influencer Ansem dumped millions of dollars worth of meme coins, which led to accusations that the trader had deliberately sold his holdings and blamed hackers.

The incident sent The Black Bull, a Solana meme coin that trades as ANSEM named after the influencer, crashing roughly 60% in less than an hour. An on-chain investigation subsequently identified $2.57 million in funds transferred to a wallet on Arbitrum.

“On November 24, we identified unauthorized transfers involving Bullpen accounts opened during our early beta between April and June 2024,” the company said on X. “Our preliminary count is 18–19 affected accounts, including [Ansem’s].”

You can now act on the news you read: Go long or short Solana with perpetual futures, all from your Decrypt Money Account.

The announcement lends credibility to Ansem's explanation of what happened earlier Tuesday, when blockchain trackers spotted his wallet rapidly liquidating its meme coin holdings.

“Pump wallet is hacked, trying to figure out how, believe its unauthorized access to my bullpen profile somehow which had the sol priv key imported,” Ansem wrote on X.

Bullpen, a crypto trading terminal co-founded by Ansem himself, allows traders to import existing wallets using their private keys. Anyone who obtains that key can effectively take control of the corresponding wallet, signing transactions that the blockchain recognizes as legitimate regardless of who initiated them.

A subsequent investigation by blockchain data provider Bitquery identified moved funds at $2.57 million total, with approximately $2.1 million coming from meme coin sales.

Ansem's explanation initially met considerable skepticism from crypto traders and blockchain researchers, some of whom pointed to what appeared to be connections between the recipient wallet and the influencer's older addresses.

“Pretty sure Ansem didn’t get hacked lol,” pseudonymous blockchain researcher MLM wrote on X.

“The onchain activity looks nothing like a hack,” he added. “Just an hour before the selling started, a previously inactive wallet I’d labeled as Ansem’s a year ago funded the wallet that later received the sale proceeds.”

A proposed Community Note on Ansem's post went considerably further, accusing the influencer of deliberately liquidating his position and transferring the proceeds to his own wallets. The note even drew a comparison with Haliey Welch, the internet celebrity behind the controversial HAWK meme coin.

The note was still awaiting additional ratings.

Ansem rose to prominence during the 2024 meme coin frenzy thanks in part to his calls on tokens such as Dogwifhat (WIF). Decrypt named him among its rising crypto stars that year, when his following had grown to approximately 600,000 accounts on X.

His namesake token debuted on the Solana meme coin factory Pump.fun in June 2026 after an anonymous developer created the coin and allocated a substantial portion of its supply to the influencer.

There were also reasons to question the accusations against Ansem before Bullpen issued its statement. Bitquery found that an older Solana wallet was emptied around the same time as his main wallet, potentially explaining why an address previously associated with the trader had funded the recipient.

Meanwhile, his Hyperliquid trading account, which held approximately $373,000, remained untouched. Someone with access exclusively to his Solana private keys would not necessarily have access to that account.

Bullpen said the affected accounts represent less than 0.005% of its registered user base. The company has yet to disclose the precise vulnerability, the total losses across affected accounts, or whether it intends to compensate users.

“We’ve taken the affected test service offline,” Bullpen said, adding that it would contact affected users directly and provide updates every three hours throughout the investigation.

#4947. Switzerland Picks 57 Countries for Crypto Tax Data Sharing Starting in 2028

Switzerland’s Federal Council has approved 57 countries and territories with which the country plans to automatically share tax information on crypto users starting in 2028, extending its long-standing bank data exchange to bitcoin and other digital assets.

The list includes all European Union member states, the United Kingdom and various G20 countries, the State Secretariat for International Finance (SIF) said in a release on Wednesday. The exchange will run under the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development’s Crypto-Asset Reporting Framework, known as CARF.

With the decision, Switzerland intends to implement the crypto exchange at the same time as other global asset management centers, according to the release. The government did not name the 57 jurisdictions beyond those broad groups, and it did not publish the full list alongside the announcement.

Data will not flow to every name on the list. An exchange will take place only if a partner jurisdiction wants to swap information with Switzerland and meets the conditions of the OECD standard, in particular its requirements on confidentiality and data security.

Before any financial account or crypto data changes hands, the Federal Council will run a targeted check of whether each partner complies with OECD standards. It will rely on a review mechanism Parliament approved on Sept. 28, 2026, which covers both the older exchange of bank account data and the new crypto exchange.

The domestic legal basis for the crypto exchange took effect on Jan. 1, 2026. Earlier this month, though, the SIF said the framework could not be implemented before Jan. 1, 2027, because the partner list still needed approval and notifications had to go to the OECD. The rules do not apply this year.

The Council also approved Armenia and Rwanda as new partners for the exchange of financial account information, with first exchanges due in 2028, and signed off on two notifications needed to carry out the exchange. Both partner lists were broadly supported during public consultations in 2024 and 2025, the government said.

The final list is shorter than first planned. In June 2025, the Federal Council proposed 74 countries relevant to the crypto market, including all EU states, the UK and most G20 members. That plan left out the United States and Saudi Arabia, and it targeted a 2026 start with first data exchanges in 2027.

Wednesday’s release did not say which countries were dropped or whether the U.S. is now on the list. The U.S. has committed to begin CARF exchanges by 2029, according to the OECD’s Global Forum, which lists Switzerland among 27 jurisdictions aiming for first exchanges by 2028.

That U.S. timeline is already shaping policy elsewhere. South Korea pushed its 22% crypto tax back to 2029 partly because it will not receive American crypto trading data until CARF exchanges with the U.S. begin that year. Officials said taxing earlier could put Korea’s domestic market at a disadvantage.

Switzerland’s decision lands as European governments debate how much they should know about crypto holders. On Tuesday, France’s Senate rejected a rule that would have forced bitcoin holders to declare self-custody wallets, while EU states began collecting crypto transaction data under the bloc’s DAC8 directive this year.

For Switzerland, CARF extends a system it already runs for bank accounts. The country has exchanged financial account information automatically under the OECD’s Common Reporting Standard since 2018, ending much of the secrecy once tied to Swiss banking. Its regulated crypto market keeps growing, with the country’s financial regulator clearing its first bitcoin ETF in October.

Under CARF, crypto service providers in Switzerland will have to collect information on users who are tax residents of activated partner jurisdictions and report it to Swiss tax authorities, which then pass it on to those partners once the exchange begins.

It also adopts an atomic delivery-versus-payment onchain settlement model, providing 24-hour settlement in multi-currencies using cash tokens.

The platform's capabilities were "validated" through trial trades in tokenized Exchange Fund Bills earlier this year, CMU OmniClear said in a separate statement.

Established in 2024, CMU OmniClear operates and develops Hong Kong’s Central Moneymarkets Unit system on behalf of the HKMA. The central securities depository had more than HK$6 trillion ($765.5 billion) in assets under custody as of the end of September.

CMU OmniClear plans to explore expanding the platform beyond debt securities to other asset classes, including funds and real-world assets, according to the statement. It will also explore opportunities to integrate with other decentralized platforms and instruments, including tokenized deposits and regulated stablecoins.

The first batch of direct participants are HSBC, Standard Chartered, Bank of China (HK), DBS, and six other banks, per the statement.

"CMU OmniClear is implementing a strategic roadmap to establish the CMU as the core infrastructure for a multi-asset digital financial ecosystem in Hong Kong," Eddie Yue, chief executive of the HKMA, said in the statement. "This also creates synergies with HKMA's digital payment initiatives, facilitating efficient and secure end-to-end processes for digital assets."

"Partnering with industry stakeholders, we will actively expand use cases, diversify asset class coverage, and connect with broader payment rails and other DLT platforms to create a future-proof ecosystem that defines the next generation of digital finance," said Stanley Chan, CEO of CMU OmniClear.

Hong Kong is ramping up efforts to develop its digital asset ecosystem, particularly as tokenized assets gain traction.

In June, the HKMA formed an expert group to drive the development of tokenized bonds. It is also exploring the use of agentic AI to monitor crypto asset transactions and detect money-laundering risks, Executive Director Raymond Chan said last week.

Elsewhere in Asia, Singapore's OCBC Bank launched a pilot with StraitsX on Monday for cross-border business-to-business stablecoin payments. Last week, the Monetary Authority of Singapore announced that it issued S$100 million ($77.5 million) of four-week tokenized MAS Bills on Nov. 6.
