#4895. A Complete Guide to Caring For Your Nails While Working Out

The gym: Great for muscle tone and cardiovascular health, less ideal for your nails. This advice will help keep your tips in top shape.

Women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in. Why Trust Us?

THE ENDORPHINS, the physical changes you can see and feel in your body, the overall confidence boost that comes with doing something good for your body—yeah, the benefits of working out are hard to beat. The one area where a sweat session can fall short, however, is when it comes to the health of our nails.

If you're someone who loves a fresh manicure, especially one with some length, you know the struggle of keeping your tips intact at the gym. Between chipped polish, cracks and peeling, and the mental gymnastics of trying to avoid both, it can sometimes feel like your nails (and your sanity) are getting a workout of their own. “When I’m lifting plates or handling weights, I’m always conscious of how I’m gripping,” shares celebrity manicurist and KISS ambassador Gina Edwards, who's a frequent gym-goer herself. “I use my finger pads rather than the tips of my fingers to help avoid putting unnecessary pressure on my nails.”

Meet the experts: Gina Edwards is a celebrity manicurist and KISS ambassador. Dana Stern, MD, is a New York-based dermatologist who specializes in nail disorders. Marisa Garshick, MD, is a dermatologist based in New York City. Jin Soon Choi is a celebrity manicurist in New York City.

Not into manicures? Unfortunately, that doesn't mean you're completely off the hook. Even bare nails can take a beating: “The nail is a thousand times more absorptive of water than the skin,” says New York dermatologist Dana Stern, MD, who specializes in nail disorders. And because frequent handwashing and exposure to moisture often go hand in hand with working out, nails are subjected to expansion as they absorb water and contraction as they dry. “Repeated wet-dry cycles can contribute to splitting and peeling, particularly in people already prone to brittle nails,” Dr Stern adds.

But not to worry—you don’t have to choose between having polished digits and getting your fitness on. With a few smart habits, you can avoid all the pitfalls. Here’s how.

No matter how you choose to work out, there are plenty of ways your nails can suffer. And most of us don't even realize we're putting them in harm's way until it's too late. Maybe you're in a workout class, engaging in some friendly competition with your neighbor to see who can knock out their burpees the fastest, only to jam a nail as your hands hit the ground. Or perhaps the damage happens before you even break a sweat. Picture it: You're pulling on your most compressive pair of leggings when a nail snags on the fabric or, worse, bends backward and breaks.

Of course, some activities pose a more obvious risk than others. Exercises that involve “repetitive gripping, pressure, or friction, such as weightlifting, rock climbing, and certain types of strength training” can be especially hard on your nails, says Marisa Garshick, MD, a dermatologist based in New York City.

Here are a few of the ways your workout routine might be doing a number on them:

Handling dumbbells, weight plates, and other equipment can put pressure on nails, especially if they're long, dry, or already weak, says celebrity manicurist Jin Soon Choi.

Jamming a nail against a hard surface or repeatedly putting pressure on it can cause the nail plate to separate from the nail bed, a condition known as onycholysis. This can happen to natural nails, too, although extensions may create additional opportunities for snagging.

When a falsie gets caught on something, it can even cause the underlying natural nail to lift from the nail bed, explains Dr. Stern. Depending on the extent of the damage, it can take months for a healthy new nail to grow in.

Frequent handwashing and exposure to harsh cleansers (including those used to wipe down gym equipment and alcohol-based hand sanitizers) can contribute to splitting and peeling, Dr. Stern adds.

While running and cycling may be gentler on your hands, repeated pressure inside athletic shoes can cause bruising beneath the nail (known as a subungual hematoma), thickening, or even nail loss, explains Dr. Garshick.

The good news? Most workout-related nail damage is temporary, provided the nail matrix, which is responsible for nail growth, hasn't been damaged. But more serious injuries can have lasting consequences. A crush injury—heavy weight falling on a nail, for example—could cause permanent damage to the nail matrix, Dr. Stern says. Even when the damage isn't permanent, patience is key. According to Dr. Garshick, fingernails typically take three to six months to grow out, while toenails can take twelve to eighteen months.

The goal isn't to give up your favorite workouts or your favorite manicures. A few tweaks to your nail-care routine and how you handle equipment can make all the difference.

Here's what the pros recommend to keep your nails looking and feeling their best.

This ultra-nourishing product delivers a healthy dose of barrier-repairing ceramides, hyaluronic acid, and niacinamide sans greasy residue.

Jinsoon Primrose + Honeysuckle Healing Cuticle Oil

Choi recommends this product, from her own line, before bed to help maintain healthy nails and cuticles.

You’ve heard of bond builders for hair, right? This is the same thing, but for nails. It promises longer, stronger nails in just four weeks.

It’s important to keep in mind that Dr. Garshick says not every nail change is workout-related. Persistent discoloration, thickening, or lifting can sometimes indicate a fungal infection, psoriasis, or another nail condition. A new or changing dark streak, particularly one that doesn't grow out, should also be evaluated by a board-certified dermatologist.

At the end of the day, you don't have to choose between crushing your fitness goals and keeping your nails in good shape. In fact, Choi points out that exercise itself can actually be beneficial for nail health, as physical activity promotes healthy circulation, helping deliver oxygen and nutrients to the tissues responsible for nail growth.

It's the accidental injuries and repeated pressure that can cause problems, not the workouts themselves. With a few simple adjustments to your nail-care routine and a bit more awareness of how you're handling equipment, you can keep breaking a sweat without breaking a nail.

Butterfill sees bitcoin trading between $60,000 and $90,000, with a breakout likely hinging on a change in Fed expectations.

Bitcoin fell more than 4% to around $57,300 on Wednesday before recovering to $59,400 as stocks sold off in the wake of U.S. data showing inflation ramping up in October.

CoinShares head of research James Butterfill said bitcoin Bitcoin (BTC) may already be near a bottom, but expects more volatility in the coming months.

The S&P 500 was down 2.6% in the first few hours of trading on Wednesday, while the total crypto market cap fell to $2.08 trillion, its lowest level since September 2024. Roughly $515 million in crypto positions were liquidated over the past 24 hours, according to CoinGlass.

Other cryptocurrencies in the top 20 were mostly on par with bitcoin. Ether fell 2.6% to $1,650, Solana Solana (SOL) was down more than 3% to $68, while Hyperliquid Hyperliquid (HYPE) fell  8% back near a three-month low of $57.

"I think we're really close to the tail end of the bear market," Butterfill said on Wednesday's episode of The Block's The Starting Block podcast. #4892. OpenAI and Anthropic Insiders Fear Their Next AI Models Are Too Dangerous to Release

OpenAI and Anthropic Insiders Fear Their Next AI Models Are Too Dangerous to Release

Employees at OpenAI and Anthropic are increasingly concerned that their companies' most advanced AI models may never be safe enough for public release, according to a Tuesday report by Axios citing more than two dozen sources familiar with internal discussions.

Some researchers believe the technical problems can eventually be solved. Others reportedly want the companies to stop training more intelligent models altogether.

The report comes two days after Meta Chief AI Officer Alexandr Wang warned that humanity might be approaching a point where it can no longer effectively supervise artificial intelligence. Wang argued that decisions made over the next year could determine whether humans retain control over increasingly autonomous, self-improving AI systems.

You can now act on the news you read: Go long or short Anthropic with perpetual futures, all from your Decrypt Money Account.

His warning followed Anthropic mathematician Levent Alpöge's announcement that an unreleased version of Claude had helped him prove the Riemann Hypothesis, a mathematical problem that had frustrated researchers for 167 years.

The same intellectual abilities that make these models so valuable for scientific research are making them harder to supervise. A model capable of spotting something that generations of mathematicians missed could conceivably spot weaknesses in a safety system that its developers overlooked.

One of the biggest problems facing AI researchers involves reinforcement learning, a training technique that rewards models for successfully completing tasks. It's largely responsible for the impressive reasoning abilities of modern AI systems, but it can also teach them to cheat.

Researchers call this reward hacking. A model might, for example, manipulate the software responsible for grading its work instead of actually solving the problem it was assigned.

Anthropic encountered a version of this problem in February, when researchers reversed three days of training on Claude Mythos Preview after discovering undesirable behaviors. An internal review later flagged more than 10% of its active training environments for problems that included opportunities for cheating and incorrectly configured tasks.

Another problem involves chain-of-thought monitoring, which allows researchers to inspect the intermediate reasoning an AI generates before producing an answer or taking an action. Some unreleased models are increasingly capable of obscuring that reasoning or generating misleading explanations that satisfy their monitors.

In other words, the explanation researchers receive may no longer accurately reflect how the model arrived at its decision.

OpenAI has already experienced the real-world consequences of inadequate containment. The company acknowledged that an internal research model was primarily responsible for compromising AI development platform Hugging Face while pursuing a difficult task.

Keeping the smartest models away from ChatGPT and Claude users would therefore address only part of the problem.

“Keeping a model internal doesn't make it safe,” an Anthropic spokesperson told Axios.

OpenAI Chief Scientist Jakub Pachocki proposed Sunday that AI developers agree on common limits to model development, based partly on perplexity—a mathematical measure of how accurately a model predicts subsequent pieces of text, with lower scores indicating better predictions.

Pachocki argues that companies should agree not to cross certain thresholds until researchers develop more effective ways of monitoring AI behavior. He estimates that AI-assisted research could substantially accelerate the development of new models as early as 2027.

Getting competing companies to voluntarily slow down could prove particularly difficult, especially as investors expect returns on the enormous amounts of money pouring into AI infrastructure. Anthropic itself raised more than $81 billion when it went public last week.

OpenAI said last week that it would suspend training or withhold models again if they failed to satisfy its safety requirements. Anthropic has separately committed to publishing a policy proposal on independent AI evaluators by December 15, followed by a framework addressing the pace of AI development by January 15, 2027.

#4891. Want to Build Muscle? These Are the 6 Protein Powders Our Editors Trust

Build muscle and fill nutritional gaps with these dietitian-approved picks.

Our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved. We may earn a commission through links on our site. Why Trust Us?

PROTEIN POWDER CAN be a powerful supplement when used correctly, like creatine or a multivitamin. But finding the right one for your needs is a big task in an overcrowded protein market. Studies show protein powders can help build lean muscle and promote optimal recovery, making them a widely sought-after supplement. It’s hard to find an easier way to make progress toward your daily protein goals than by taking a few big gulps of a high-protein smoothie. But protein powder is not just a vehicle for hitting your protein goals—many powders also contain other beneficial nutrients, like iron, calcium, fiber, and sometimes even vitamin D.

There are multiple types of protein powder to sift through, the most common being whey protein. Whey protein is derived from cow’s milk and is the most widely consumed type of protein powder. In addition to whey, you’ll find casein protein (also derived from cow’s milk but slower to digest than whey), and plant-based proteins (rice, pea, hemp, pumpkin seed, or a blend of these).

Overall, the best protein powders keep it simple: They boast a solid macronutrient profile and taste great. While there are other factors that should be in consideration throughout your search (i.e., third-party testing, type of protein, and price), if you stick to those two basics, you’re likely to find a powder you can easily and consistently implement into your daily routine. Do you need to slam a protein shake as soon as you finish working out? No.

Other lists out there have too many picks, in our opinion, and we're only looking to share with you the very best of what we've found. Our in-house testers have put dozens of protein powders through the blender (and shaker) for years, not months, and dubbed these six as their favorites. The same could be said for the expert nutritionists we consulted with, like Jordan Sullivan, who's worked with UFC champions like Israel Adesanya and Alex Volkanovski. If you’re on the hunt for a reliable protein powder and want the tedious testing work done for you, read below for our top picks for the best protein powders.

I'm a NASM-certified nutritionist who has spent years covering the intersection of fitness and nutrition. I started with input from the Men's Health editors, including Fitness and Reviews Editor Charles Thorp, NASM, Senior Fitness Editor Brett Williams, NASM, and Fitness Director Ebenezer Samuel, C.S.C.S. Our team spent hundreds of hours testing products, interviewing registered dietitians, medical doctors, fitness professionals, athletes of all kinds (some of whom shared their insights below), and our own Advisory Board.

The testing pool started with the top-rated and bestselling protein powders on the market, then was cut down from there. The products that made it into this guide undergo third-party testing, hold an NSF, USP, or Informed Sport certification, and contain standardized forms of protein in clinically studied, safe amounts.

We considered every nutrition label, ingredient list, price, and many reviews from certified buyers. We made and drank hundreds of post-workout protein smoothies as part of our examination process. The list below represents our thoughtful picks of the very best protein powders to help with your gains in 2026.

The brand name doesn’t lie here—Transparent Labs lists all ingredients clearly on the label and unlike some other protein brands, it doesn’t include ingredients you can’t pronounce. Without fillers or artificial ingredients, you’re left with the important stuff: 28 grams of whey protein isolate, only 1 gram each of carbs and fat, and just 130 calories. You’ll also find a touch of three micronutrients (we’re talking less than 9 percent of your recommended daily value), calcium, iron, and potassium. Another perk? This protein powder is sweetened with stevia extract, so you won’t find any added sugar here.

Men’s Health Fitness and Commerce Editor Charles Thorp, NASM, tested the product personally and says, "it was a refreshing surprise to try a product without unnecessary junk in it. The high-protein content of this product let's me hit my intake goals with ease, and also tastes great."

All that said, Transparent Labs Whey Protein Isolate is sourced from grass-fed dairy, so it won’t be suitable for vegans. And a protein that’s as clean as this one comes with a higher price tag. While the average protein powder on this list costs closer to $1.50 per serving, TL will run you $2.00 a serving. But for us, Transparent Labs’ high protein content per scoop and lack of filler ingredients is well worth the extra 50 cents.

When looking for the best protein powder for athletes of all ages, we want two things: First, we need an all-around solid product that boasts ample protein. Second, we need a product that is thoroughly third-party tested and certified safe for competitive athletes. Thorne Whey Protein Isolate ticks both of those boxes, and it also happens to taste great, according to Thorp.

Thorp didn’t just test this product for this review. "Thorne is one of the supplement brands I have used the most, and its protein powder has been a mainstay in my routine," he says. And for good reason: It boasts 21 grams of bioavailable whey protein isolate, and just 4 grams of carbs, 1 gram of fat, and 100 calories. With such a low calorie count, you can also mix this powder with other ingredients (fruit, peanut butter, etc.) to create a hearty, protein-packed smoothie.

"The taste of the chocolate flavor is smooth, and blends well with any fruit or additional nutrition you want to add, or just on its own with water or milk," Thorp says. "There is a mild amount of sweetness, but it doesn’t overpower. The result is pretty pleasant as far as taste.”

While the flavor and macros are great, it’s worth noting that this protein does contain gums, which some athletes may avoid. Thorne also costs a bit more than average at $2.17 per serving—but if you’re a competitive athlete looking for a certified product, that extra cost should provide the assurance you need.

If you’ve been hunting for the right protein powder for a while, it’s likely you’ve come across Optimum Nutrition Gold Standard 100% Whey in the process. Optimum Nutrition is one of the most widely known (and used) protein brands—take it from Thorp, who initially started his fitness journey taking Optimum Nutrition Gold Standard. One of the biggest draws for newbies just testing the waters (and financially savvy folks in general)? The price point.

Depending on the jug size (the bigger you go, the cheaper the cost per serving), your price per scoop can be as low as $1.06 with the highest you’ll pay for a scoop from a smaller container being only $1.54. How does the brand keep the cost lower than the market average? Thorp explains, “It's not a pure whey protein isolate (it's a blend) and depending on your stomach, you'll realize this fast.” (Sensitive stomachs may want to lean toward a less dairy-heavy whey isolate.)

But if the whey isolate, whey concentrate, and hydrolyzed whey protein blend is not an issue for your digestive system, this is a great straightforward option featuring 24 grams of protein and 5.5 grams of BCAAs. Just make sure you’re mixing with milk or in a smoothie as we did find this powder to have a synthetic aftertaste in testing when we mixed it solely with water.

If you’ve been to your local health foods store, you’ve likely seen Orgain Organic Plant Based Protein Powder. Thorp can attest, "I first started using Orgain when I went vegan for a few years," he says. "This was back when there weren't as many vegan protein powder options as there are now. I liked how accessible it was, through both Amazon (usually at some sort of discount) and at my local Whole Foods."

Aside from being easy to attain, Orgain is also made with a plant protein blend, which provides a full amino acid profile—a trait sometimes difficult to come across in vegan protein powders. The taste is also reliable. Thorp found the flavor lighter than some of the other protein powders he has tested in his over 10 years working in the supplement space. He also noted that it blends better than most vegan powders with a smooth and creamy mouthfeel, rather than a gritty one.

Though this powder packs 21 grams of protein, it also contains 15 grams of carbs and 3.5 grams of fat, which is higher than your typical whey protein. While this may not be ideal for those on a cut, Thorp offers a different perspective: "While it has more carbs and fats than others, that could be a positive for anyone looking to really supplement their diet in a larger way. [This nutrition profile] makes it a more satisfying drink." And with that, it’s important to note that a full serving is two scoops, so you may need to blend with a little more water or milk than normal to make sure the texture is not overly thick.

If taste is your number one priority, Dymatize ISO100 should be your number one pick. MH Fitness Director Ebenezer Samuel, C.S.C.S., also stands by this protein powder. "It's nutritional profile is great," he says. "That's why this Dymatize is the only protein I use."

“The flavor is top-notch. [Dymatize] is among the most consistently best-tasting wheys, regardless of the specific flavor," says Fitness Editor Cori Ritchey.

Ritchey also noted that her sensitive stomach had no qualms with this hydrolyzed whey protein isolate, which is a testament to the product’s hydrolyzed form. Whey protein isolate is whey protein that has already been broken down into smaller peptides for easier digestion, but hydrolysis takes that processing a step further—studies show the absorption level is even higher in hydrolyzed whey isolate.

With 25 grams of protein and only 120 calories, this is a great lean protein option. Just note that there are artificial flavors and gums, which some may avoid for digestive purposes.

If you’re vegan, lactose-intolerant, or just want to add a little variety to your protein sources, Transparent Labs is pulling through. Transparent Labs Organic Vegan Protein is our favorite vegan protein powder for two reasons: One, it is a blend of pea and rice protein, which studies have shown offers a complete protein (similar to a whey) with a full amino acid profile. You'll find if you decide to go with just a pea protein product, you'll likely still be recommended to take it with a rice product as well. And two, it boasts 15 percent of your recommended daily iron, which studies show some vegans may be deficient in.

This vegan protein also packs a higher protein content per serving than most vegan powders—24 grams compared to the more typical 20 grams. Thorp tested Transparent Labs Organic Vegan Protein and thinks it’s a great option not just for vegans, but for anyone looking for a different source of protein. "This is one of my favorite proteins around, and it [just] happens to be vegan, for any of those living by that diet or [who are] lactose intolerant. Also, if your diet already has a lot of dairy in it, using this protein powder can help to diversify your intake," he notes.

It is also worth noting that though Transparent Labs Whey Isolate comes in a wide variety of flavors, the flavor options for the pea protein and rice protein products are more limited—just chocolate or vanilla.

There are three main types of protein powder to consider: whey protein, casein protein, and plant-based protein. You’ve probably seen whey protein the most—it’s derived from cow’s milk and comes in the form of whey concentrate, whey isolate, or hydrolyzed whey. Whey concentrate is the least processed form of whey protein, and therefore, contains the most dairy. Whey isolate is processed to remove most of the dairy, and hydrolyzed whey is processed even further for the best absorption of the three, according to studies.

Casein protein is also derived from cow’s milk, but it is much slower to digest than whey protein. Some people even take casein at night, so it has time to process as they sleep, according to some studies. Plant-based protein is derived from plant-based sources like rice, pea, hemp, pumpkin seed, or a combination of these. It can be higher in carbs and a touch lower in protein because of this, but proteins made of a blend of plant sources typically provide a similar nutritional profile to whey proteins. There is no right or wrong answer when it comes to the type of protein you should seek out—it just comes down to what you’re best able to implement into your fitness routine and daily lifestyle.

A good protein powder typically offers anywhere from 20 to 30 grams of protein per scoop. Plant-based powders often sit on the lower end of this range with whey and casein being on the higher end. You’ll want to consider how much protein you want from your shakes vs. your whole food meals. If you’re looking to use a protein powder as part of a smoothie for a meal replacement, you’ll want a powder closer to 30 grams of protein, according to studies. If you’re just looking to use a protein shake as a snack, that 20 grams range will work just fine.

While protein is the main character, fats, carbs, and calories are also important considerations. If you’re looking to build lean muscle, you’ll want a protein powder that’s low in all three—it’s surprisingly easy to find a protein powder with three or fewer grams of both fat and carbs, especially whey isolates and hydrolyzed wheys. If you're bulking it could even be tempting to try a protein powder that's high in carbs, fats, and calories, but you will never accomplish the same quality of nutrition you get out of actual food. Better to focus on getting a quality protein powder and grab a quick real meal when you can.

While all of the products we talk about on this list are third-party tested, this certification is a big factor to consider when hunting for supplements. Many supplements don’t provide third-party testing (protein powders included), and since supplements aren’t FDA-regulated, there’s no way to know if what’s on the product’s label is actually what’s in the product without third-party testing. Be sure to take this into account when considering any supplement purchase.

Your average protein powder will cost anywhere from $1.00 to $2.00 per serving, with most falling right in the middle around $1.50 per serving. The more expensive powders are typically cleaner, boasting all-natural ingredients, no additives, a higher protein content, and thorough third-party testing. The less expensive options may contain more artificial ingredients, have a lower protein content, and/or offer no third-party testing. Compare prices and ingredients across this list (and throughout the market) to find the best value product for your lifestyle and budget.

While most athletes focus on the big three (protein, fat, carbs), micronutrients should not be overlooked—especially if you follow a specific diet (like vegan or keto). Protein powders can be a great source of other nutrients like iron, calcium, vitamin D, and potassium. These micronutrients may be more important to those who don’t get them as much from their regular diet (vegans, for example, often don’t get enough iron in their regular meals). But according to studies, it’s also a good idea to pay attention to these ingredients to ensure you’re not consuming an overkill amount of any particular micronutrient.

If you’re finding it difficult to get enough protein in your daily diet, protein powders can help. They’re a convenient way to help hit your protein goals—easier than downing four or five chicken breasts a day, at least.

Getting enough protein in your diet can help you build lean muscle and recover better after your workouts. This is thanks to amino acids (the building blocks of protein), which help stimulate muscle protein synthesis. Studies show during muscle protein synthesis, the body uses these amino acids to repair muscle tissue after your workouts—i.e. your body’s way of building muscle.

If you’re following a solid workout regimen, protein powders can be a great way to sneak in some additional protein on top of your whole food diet. Studies show protein can help you stay fuller for longer, too. But remember that protein powders are meant to be a supplement, meaning you should still be getting most of your protein from whole food sources.

Protein powders can contain additional ingredients—like artificial flavors or sweeteners, fillers or gums, allergens, and/or added sugars—that some customers may try to avoid. The key with these types of ingredients is moderation.

While artificial flavors and sweeteners haven’t been proven harmful in moderation, there isn’t enough evidence on how consuming them consistently can impact long-term health. Gums and fillers should also be consumed in moderation as they can cause digestive issues. Like artificial flavors/sweeteners, there’s also a broader concern over the long-term effects these ingredients may have, but more research is needed. Added sugars—ingredients like table sugar, high-fructose corn syrup, corn syrup, honey, molasses, and fruit juice concentrates—are also best in moderation, as they’re high in calories but offer no real nutritional value. Studies show added sugar should make up less than 10 percent of your daily calories.

Allergens—like gluten, dairy, or nuts—are the only ingredients you’ll want to avoid entirely if you have a specific food sensitivity. Dairy is probably the most relevant one with protein powders as most whey and casein products do contain dairy (even if it’s in trace amounts).

The settlement was filed Nov. 24 in the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of California, bringing a seven-year legal battle closer to a conclusion.

Nvidia has agreed to pay $290 million to settle a long-running securities class-action lawsuit alleging it misled investors about the extent of cryptocurrency mining demand contributing to its gaming GPU sales in 2017 and 2018.

The proposed settlement, which still requires court approval, resolves claims that Nvidia and CEO Jensen Huang understated crypto miners' contributions to gaming revenue and failed to disclose the risks posed by a subsequent collapse in mining demand, driven largely by a slump in Ethereum mining. Plaintiffs alleged that the disclosures contributed to a 28.5% drop in Nvidia's stock over two trading sessions in November 2018.

Nvidia said its insurers are funding the majority of the $290 million settlement, while plaintiffs' attorneys are requesting up to $62 million in legal fees from the fund.

The settlement was filed Nov. 24 in the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of California, bringing a seven-year legal battle closer to a conclusion.

The case was dismissed in 2021 but revived by the Ninth Circuit in 2023, and a federal judge certified it as a class action earlier this year.

In a separate case, Nvidia settled with the Securities and Exchange Commission for $5.5 million over similar disclosures concerning the impact of crypto mining on its gaming business.

The settlement comes amid a volatile month for Nvidia, the world's most valuable company.

Nvidia's stock (NVDA) has swung sharply following reports earlier this month that cofounder and longtime CEO Jensen Huang had resigned amid allegations of multiple affairs, including one with an alleged Chinese spy.

The board subsequently voted to reinstate Huang on Monday, sending the stock surging more than 30% before renewed selling pressure hit the broader technology sector as concerns over AI valuations rattled markets.

#4887. Take-Two Hits GTA 6 PC Port Leonida With DMCA, Taking Down 3,007 GitHub Repos

Take-Two Hits GTA 6 PC Port Leonida With DMCA, Taking Down 3,007 GitHub Repos

Take-Two Interactive has used a copyright takedown notice to remove Leonida, one of the most prominent projects attempting to port the leaked Xbox build of Grand Theft Auto 6 to PC, along with thousands of copies of its code.

GitHub published a Digital Millennium Copyright Act (DMCA) notice from Take-Two's IP Enforcement Team on Tuesday. Because the publisher alleged that all or most of the project's forks infringed to the same extent as the original, GitHub said it processed the takedown against the entire network of 3,007 repositories.

The notice clears up why the project disappeared on Monday. Its GitHub page had shown an error page rather than a DMCA notice, so it was initially unclear whether it had been removed by its creator or by Take-Two.

The project described itself as "a native PC recompilation of the Xbox version of Grand Theft Auto 6." Take-Two said it reproduced copyrighted elements of the game and was a derivative work, breaching Rockstar's terms of service, which bar users from decompiling, reverse engineering or creating derivative works from its games.

Leonida did not include the leaked game files itself. Instead, its instructions told users to supply their own Xbox Series files.

Take-Two dismissed that approach. Stolen files from an Xbox Series build of the game were publicly distributed on November 20, 2026, and Leonida's repository opened the following day, it said.

"The instruction to 'bring your own files' attempts to shift the responsibility for supplying files to the user and to make it seems as if this is a general-purpose project," Take-Two wrote. "This is intentionally misleading."

The timing and the project's "explicit focus" on Grand Theft Auto showed the files users needed were the leaked ones, and that its developers knew it, Take-Two added. It asked GitHub to disable the repository and all its forks.

Take-Two has made the same argument before. On November 18, GitHub published four Take-Two notices against unofficial ports of GTA V to mobile devices, Macs and web browsers, three of which told users to supply their own game files. In each, Take-Two said such disclaimers "do not automatically shield" developers from secondary copyright liability when they knowingly facilitate infringement.

The project's pseudonymous creator also posted a screenshot of a Discord notice saying his server had broken the platform's rules on copyright infringement, limiting his access to servers until November 30, 2026.

He later tweeted that he was no longer working on the project "because of T2," but that "there are and always will be more projects." On Wednesday, he told followers to ignore his earlier posts, adding: "Something's coming soon."

Ignore my other posts. Something’s coming soon 👀

— NotRexed (@ItsNotRexed) November 25, 2026

The takedown follows the release of the build's main executable by leaker Cyberleek on Monday. Cyberleek had promised to release the file if the CYBERLEEK meme coin reached a $15 million market cap. The token fell short, but Cyberleek released the file anyway, and porting projects expected a playable version within days.

Take-Two has pursued the leaks for months, subpoenaing Discord and Microsoft, which owns GitHub, in August for data that could help identify Cyberleek. Rockstar has not announced a PC version of GTA 6.

#4886. How To Build Strength You’ll Actually Use In Daily Life, According To A Trainer

Strength training isn't just about what you can lift in the gym. It helps make everyday tasks easier, whether that's carrying heavy shopping bags and moving furniture or putting a suitcase in the overhead compartment on a flight.

As we get older, we naturally start to lose muscle mass, strength and bone density—at approximately 3-8% per decade after the age of 30—but regular strength training can help slow this down, reminds Andy Carr, trainer and head of fitness for Snap Fitness UK.

Thankfully, you don't need complicated exercises to see the benefits.

By focusing on simple, functional movements that mimic everyday activities, you can build strength that carries over into daily life and keeps you strong, active and confident as you get older.

“It's not necessary to spend hours lifting weights to build strength that makes a difference,” he explains. “Even two or three strength sessions a week can help, especially when you're focusing on compound exercises that work several muscle groups at once.”

Squats are one of the best exercises for building lower-body strength because—as a compound exercise—they work your thighs, glutes, and core all at once.

“These are the muscles you use when getting up from a chair, lifting something off the floor or crouching down to do some gardening,” says Carr. Keeping them strong can make a real difference to how easily you move around, particularly as you get older.

Step-ups are great for building leg strength and improving balance at the same time, says Carr.

“They're particularly useful for everyday activities like climbing stairs, walking uphill, or stepping onto curbs. As we age, maintaining strength and stability in our legs becomes increasingly important, and step-ups are a simple way to work on both,” he adds.

Farmer's carries are a brilliant exercise for building strength you actually use, because they're essentially the same movement as carrying heavy shopping bags.

“They work your grip, shoulders and core, helping you carry things more comfortably and with better stability. Grip strength can decline with age, so it's a really useful exercise to include in your routine,” says Carr.

Picking something up, whether it's a laundry basket, a suitcase or a bag of compost in the garden, involves your glutes, hamstrings, and back. Deadlifts strengthen all these muscles, explains Carr.

“They're a great way to build strength for everyday lifting, so those jobs feel easier and you're more confident handling heavier objects.”

Rows are ideal for strengthening your upper back and arms, which we use for pulling movements throughout the day, from opening heavy doors to pulling a garden hose across the lawn.

“They also help support good posture, particularly if you spend a lot of time sitting at a desk,” says Carr. “Using a resistance band makes it easy to adjust the difficulty as you get stronger.”

Incline push-ups are a great way to build upper-body strength, working your chest, shoulders, arms, and core.

“These muscles help with everyday pushing movements, whether that's moving a shopping cart, pushing open a heavy door, or getting yourself up from the floor,” says Carr.

They're also easy to adapt to your fitness level, so you can gradually increase the challenge as your strength improves.

We use rotational movements more than we probably realize, whether that's turning to put something in the back of the car, reaching across to pick something up or digging in the garden.

Woodchops are great for strengthening your core and improving your ability to twist and turn with control, Carr explains.

“That becomes particularly useful as we get older, helping us stay mobile and making everyday movements feel easier.”

On Tuesday, the DOJ said it targeted more than 800 defendants and helped law enforcement in almost a dozen countries in raids on scam call centers and compounds.

Following President Donald Trump's directive to crack down on fraud and predatory schemes, the Justice Department announced what it called its "largest-ever crackdown," targeting scammers in Southeast Asia and bad actors using digital assets to launder billions of dollars.

On Tuesday, the DOJ said it targeted more than 800 defendants and helped law enforcement in almost a dozen countries in raids on scam call centers and compounds.

"The unprecedented results of this surge are just the beginning," said Attorney General Todd Blanche in a statement. "We will continue prosecuting those who perpetrate these schemes and disrupting the activities of transnational criminal organizations before they reach American shores."

In March, Trump signed an executive order directing the Secretary of State, the Attorney General, and other officials to review their regulatory frameworks to figure out how best to combat crime, particularly related to cyber and predatory schemes against people in the U.S. Trump specifically directed Blanche to prioritize crime involving scam centers.

One of those cases was against Cambodia-based Huione Group, an organization that had been accused of laundering billions of dollars in crypto fraud proceeds. In June, the Justice Department said it had seized a cloud computing account, which it said had been used as "a technological backbone that allowed billions in fraud proceeds to be transferred, moved, and concealed," often through Southeast Asian scam centers.

The State Department also funded efforts by U.S. and Southeast Asian law enforcement to help freeze more than $1 billion in stolen crypto, the DOJ said Tuesday.

"State Department-funded forensic tools helped analyze more than 10,000 devices and hard drives in Thailand alone, allowing U.S. and Thai law enforcement to better understand the criminal networks and advance U.S. investigations," the DOJ said.

The State Department also targeted Moldova, where it trained local prosecutors and provided equipment that then helped with raids in October that ended in the closure of five call centers and five people arrested for allegedly running a fake crypto trading platform, according to the DOJ.

The crackdown comes as the Trump administration has pursued a largely pro-crypto agenda, pledging to make the U.S. the global capital of the digital asset industry and rolling back regulations it views as limiting innovation. But that approach has drawn criticism from lawmakers, particularly over Trump's personal and family-linked crypto ventures and potential conflicts of interest.

#4884. The 11 Best War Movies About Brotherhood, Ranked

Our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved. We may earn a commission through links on our site. Why Trust Us?

Ahead of Netflix’s The Mosquito Bowl, we’ve pulled together a list of gripping films that show how bonds between men survive—and sometimes break—under fire.

DIRECTOR PETER BERG had never made a World War II movie before The Mosquito Bowl, but he certainly knows a thing or two about football. The director of Friday Night Lights has returned to a world of cocksure young players with their whole lives ahead of them in dire need of rousing their morale—only now it’s the true story of the football game between two World War II Marine regiments at Guadalcanal on Christmas Eve 1944. There’s another connection: both The Mosquito Bowl and Friday Night Lights are adapted from books by author Buzz Bissinger.

Berg’s new Netflix film dramatizes the stories of football players John McLaughry (Nicholas Galitzine), Tony Butkovich (Ray Nicholson), Bob Bauman (Bill Skarsgård), and Dave Schreiner (Tom Francis), who traded the NFL draft for military service. After enduring years of the Pacific campaign, they realize how valuable the team spirit and camaraderie of football can be as the Battle of Okinawa looms ahead of them.

The Mosquito Bowl underlines the devastating impact WWII’s casualty count had on an entire generation of young athletes, and the film unites its twin focuses of war and football by their mutual sense of brotherhood. The deeply felt connection between soldiers is the lifeblood of historical war films; when done convincingly, a squad’s well-earned devotion and loyalty add rich melodrama to the action. Brotherhood is just as compelling when it is subverted—like the respect felt between soldiers on opposing sides, or when hardened, broken combatants struggle to express the empathy and compassion they feel. The best war movies know that brotherhood endures after the fighting stops, but in different forms—softer, stranger, when it’s hard to reconcile the memories of war with a world that continues as normal.

To mark the Thanksgiving release of The Mosquito Bowl on Netflix, we ranked the most gripping and rousing war films about brotherhood.

An ensemble of actors you'd typically see in a "Young Stars of Tomorrow" profile immerse themselves in a U.S. Navy SEAL platoon and recreate a real-time Iraq War firefight that co-director Ray Mendoza was a part of. Opening with the platoon jubilantly dancing to "Call On Me" streamed through their base's crappy internet, Warfare quickly adopts a stripped-back and meticulous play-by-play of how one slice of warfare was actually experienced. You get a sense of brotherhood from the practiced, reflexive interactions between SEALs, and their interdependence also helped build the film, as Mendoza and co-director Alex Garland drew from the testimonies of his fellow soldiers when writing the script. The stylistic choices—like a thundering sound mix and infrequent use of satellite photography—add an extra layer of tension to Warfare's depiction of courage under fire. It’s one of the most visceral movies in recent memory about modern war.

Before he brought us high-octane visions of robot cops and ambitious showgirls, Paul Verhoeven directed a handful of smash hits in his native Netherlands, including this Golden Globe-nominated war epic about the diverging fates of Dutch students during the Nazi occupation. Led by a supremely dashing Rutger Hauer, Soldier of Orange begins in 1938 and follows the wartime trajectory of Erik Lanshof, an initially neutral but increasingly principled aristocrat who protects his Dutch Resistance friends and distances himself from fascist collaborators. Before long, his entire school group has pledged one type of loyalty or another. Observed over a period of time, war reveals everything, and Erik’s blossoming heroism emerges as a result of his friendships all changing—for better or worse.

Forgive us for taking a creative approach to the headline so early in the list: Hell in the Pacific features no battles or squadron camaraderie, and takes place on a deserted island with only two characters—an American pilot (Lee Marvin) and a Japanese army captain (Toshiro Mifune)—who don’t understand a word the other person says. Even without comprehension, the American and Japanese soldiers find a hundred ways to rile each other up, including shock tactics, sabotage, pranks, and even makeshift imprisonment. Gradually, they realize each other’s company is the strongest connection to their starving humanity available to them, even if they’re affected in a way they can’t explain. Free from the rhetoric and politics of war, Marvin and Mifune play men who slip into a state of brash, stubborn childishness, and a brotherly kinship forms in spite of their inherent opposition.

Clint Eastwood and Steven Spielberg sound like an odd pair to collaborate on a war picture, but Eastwood’s pared-down, melancholic visual style is a terrific fit for this post-Band of Brothers war movie. Flags of Our Fathers wasn’t received as positively as its Japanese-language companion film Letters from Iwo Jima, but it’s a robust and affecting watch—splitting its runtime between the overwhelming Battle of Iwo Jima and its aftermath, where three soldiers celebrated as the iconic “flag-raisers” spent the final year of the Pacific Campaign on a spiritually draining propaganda tour. Flags of Our Fathers takes the essential themes of war cinema—brotherhood, sacrifice, heroism—and juxtaposes them with the United States military manufacturing their own national images and narratives in real time. The tension between the brutal experience of being a brother-in-arms and the sanitized version promoted by war’s survivors makes for a powerful watch.

It’s as if director David Ayer (Suicide Squad, Bright) made a WWII movie to hammer home two points: tank warfare was a nightmare, and soldier hazing was way more hardcore than what you see in Band of Brothers. In the final months of the war in Europe, Wardaddy (Brad Pitt) rolls his bloody and battered tank unit slowly toward Berlin, and the arrival of fresh-faced pencil-pusher Norman (Logan Lerman) gives the hardened squad a chance to berate and bully the newcomer about all the ways he is soft, and war is hell. As their fellow brothers-in-arms are increasingly blasted apart into viscera, Wardaddy’s take-no-shit squad bolsters their unsentimental unity, and each of the five traumatized brothers rely on each other to watch their back and keep them sane on a frontline that might as well be the border to hell.

Spike Lee’s bracing film about the scars of Vietnam takes a familiar concept—a jaded band of veterans who try to pull off a heist—and spins it in a thorny, unpredictable direction. Four older Black veterans (led by an intense, captivating, and Oscar-snubbed Delroy Lindo) return to ‘Nam to recover the CIA gold their squadron hid during the war—aside from a delayed payday, it’s also the ultimate memorial of their late squad leader Norman (Chadwick Boseman). Marked by years of bitterness and PTSD, the “Bloods” retrace their steps while juggling painful reflections on how the war left them angry and guilty. When they're ambushed in the jungle and have to pick up guns again, we're reminded that Lee is never satisfied sticking in one narrative mode for too long, but the jagged catharsis of cranky, once-loyal soldiers confronting their wounds is far more visceral to watch.

When Private Alex (Harry Styles) says, “We're regimental brothers, mate,” in the belly of a fishing trawler on Dunkirk Beach, he’s not acting nobly—he’s making the case for throwing a soldier he thinks is German (he’s actually French) to the Nazis surrounding them. So much of Christopher Nolan’s war film about the perilous evacuation of Allied troops from France’s northernmost beaches centers on division: soldier feuds, breakdowns in communication, and a nonlinear narrative that takes place over a week or an hour depending on who’s in front of the camera. But Dunkirk’s staggering disaster and survival action builds to an overwhelming climactic sense of unity. Across every mini-arc and timeline, Nolan shows us countless pairs of soldiers, pilots, and civilians who stand together as symbolic brothers.

After the famously gnarly and disorienting D-Day beach landing sequence—which has influenced every WWII action movie since, including The Mosquito Bowl—Saving Private Ryan settles into the most iconic band of brothers story outside of… well, Band of Brothers, co-created by this film’s director and star. Tom Hanks is the grouchy uncle leading a reluctant squad to rescue Private James Francis Ryan (Matt Damon) from the front lines after his brothers were killed in action. The squadron's trudge through France is fueled with banter, grumbling, and the type of resentment that stews between siblings who hate when someone receives special treatment. Steven Spielberg’s gift for balancing movie-star gravitas and off-the-cuff charisma is on full display in the ensemble, but no gruff, hot-tempered soldier has a response to Private Ryan's justification for not returning to his mom: “Tell her that when you found me, I was here, and I was with the only brothers I have left.”

The only war film on this list to be set before the 20th century and at sea, the Napoleonic Wars-era Master and Commander has a reputation for being a “dudes/gentlemen rock” classic: the reputation still holds up. Under the command of Captain Jack Aubrey (Russell Crowe), the HMS Surprise wages war against a French frigate that taunts the crew across the seas. Majestic naval battles aside, much of Master and Commander has a warm hangout tone, focusing on the kinship between Aubrey and ship’s surgeon Maturin, their interest in classical music and botanical science, and revelrous suppers in the captain’s quarters. It's impossible to watch Peter Weir’s sea epic and not pine for the brotherly loyalty (maybe not the seasickness or cannonball attacks) that Aubrey inspires here. Nothing will make you feel the romantic thrill of adventure like Master and Commander.

Pick your favorite scene from The Deer Hunter: the riotous wedding party, the spontaneous Frankie Valli singalong over a game of pool, or the exacting game of Russian roulette played by prisoners of war. They each shine a light on the ordinary, working-class brotherhood that was completely transformed by the Vietnam War. This Oscar-winning epic builds complex, traumatized characters (played by Robert De Niro, John Cazale, and Christopher Walken) who reckon with never being able to experience their relationships and community in the same way again. The Deer Hunter paints such a disturbing and fragile picture of the “before and after” of Vietnam, as each brotherly bond becomes charged with alienation and despair. Notorious for its multiple “death game” sequences, The Deer Hunter excels in making its harrowing portrayal of war and PTSD genuinely heartbreaking.

One of the best things to come out of legendary Hong Kong filmmakers John Woo and Tsui Hark falling out was the future director of Hard Boiled and Face/Off leaving the iconic A Better Tomorrow series to make this searing war story. Beginning in the late ’60s, it focuses on three close friends (Tony Leung, Jacky Cheung, Waise Lee) whose smuggling ambitions dunk them headfirst in the brutality and desperation of the Vietnam War. Bullet in the Head blends the epic sweep of New Hollywood war epics (Apocalypse Now, The Deer Hunter) with Woo’s “heroic bloodshed” toolkit, which meant electric action spectacle and bold, tragic melodrama. An underrated operatic beast in Woo’s stacked filmography—not to mention a personal one, as Woo used the film to express his reaction to the 1989 Tiananmen Square massacre—the action is always in service of a high-stakes tri-friendship that can only take so much passion and betrayal before the treasured brotherhood breaks.

#4880. Fidelity files for spot Chainlink ETF with planned Nasdaq listing

Looking for institutional-grade crypto trading? Discover LMAX Digital, the regulated exchange from LMAX Group

The proposed fund would hold LINK directly without staking it and is expected to trade on Nasdaq under the ticker FLNK.

Financial services giant Fidelity has filed with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission to launch a spot Chainlink exchange-traded fund.

The proposed Fidelity Chainlink Fund would hold LINK directly and aim to track its price, minus the fund's expenses, according to a Form S-1 filed Wednesday. The fund is expected to trade on Nasdaq under the ticker FLNK.

LINK is the native token of Chainlink, an oracle network that helps blockchain applications access external data, such as asset prices, and communicate with other blockchains. LINK holders can also stake their tokens to earn rewards. Fidelity, however, does not plan to stake the LINK held by its proposed fund.

"The Trust will not stake its LINK, and Shareholders will not receive staking rewards through the Trust," Fidelity said in the filing.

Anchorage Digital Bank, BitGo Bank & Trust and Coinbase Custody would serve as custodians for the fund's LINK. Authorized participants would be able to create and redeem large blocks of ETF shares using either LINK or cash. The filing does not mention when the fund could begin trading.

Grayscale and Bitwise already offer U.S. spot Chainlink ETFs. As of Nov. 24, the Grayscale Chainlink Trust ETF (GLNK) had about $112 million in assets under management, and the Bitwise Chainlink ETF (CLNK) had about $42 million.

Fidelity currently offers three spot crypto ETFs in the U.S. covering bitcoin, ether, and Solana. These include the Fidelity Wise Origin Bitcoin Fund (FBTC), the Fidelity Ethereum Fund (FETH), and the Fidelity Solana Fund (FSOL). Unlike the proposed Chainlink fund, Fidelity's Solana fund, which began trading in November 2025, stakes its tokens.

The Chainlink ETF filing comes a day after Fidelity expanded the number of cryptocurrencies available for trading on its Fidelity Crypto platform, adding Chainlink's LINK, Aave's AAVE, and Uniswap's UNI.

Fidelity also entered the stablecoin market earlier this year, launching its first U.S. dollar-backed stablecoin, Fidelity Digital Dollar (FIDD), on Ethereum in February.

#4878. Hyperliquid Leads Altcoin Losses as Bitcoin Slips Below $59K

Hyperliquid Leads Altcoin Losses as Bitcoin Slips Below $59K

Hyperliquid's HYPE token led crypto's latest leg down on Wednesday, as one of the exchange's most profitable traders shut down its operations there.

HYPE fell 8.2% over 24 hours to $57.86, the steepest drop among the 20 largest cryptocurrencies by market cap, and is down 15.8% over the past week, according to Decrypt data. Bitcoin slipped 1.7% over the same period to $58,801, and Ethereum lost 2.4%, extending a sell-off that has spread across risk assets.

You can now act on the news you read: Go long or short HYPE with perpetual futures, all from your Decrypt Money Account.

Abraxas Capital has withdrawn its remaining funds from Hyperliquid and closed its entire book, almost two years after it started trading there, pseudonymous onchain analyst MLM said on Telegram on Tuesday.

The firm traded $13.4 billion on Hyperliquid and made $530 million, including at least $67 million from funding payments, according to MLM. The positions were one leg of a market-neutral strategy for its Elysium Global Arbitrage Fund, the analyst said.

Two Hyperliquid accounts labeled as Abraxas Capital on analytics platform Hyperdash have recorded combined all-time profits of more than $550 million, and now hold just over $5,000 between them, Hyperdash data shows. On Tuesday, the two accounts unstaked about 219,000 HYPE, worth roughly $12.7 million at current prices, and sent it elsewhere.

"With HYPE, upcoming token unlocks could be adding extra pressure," Eric Andersson, co-founder of Byrrgis, told Decrypt. "Altcoins tend to get hit even harder in these situations."

U.S. spot Bitcoin ETFs recorded $231.6 million in net outflows on Tuesday, their sixth consecutive day of withdrawals, according to SoSoValue data. Outflows over those six trading days total $2.6 billion.

That takes November's net outflows to $4.94 billion, surpassing June 2026's $4.51 billion as the funds' worst month since they launched in January 2024. Total net assets stand at $72 billion.

Andersson pointed to ETF outflows, uncertainty over interest rates, liquidations and weaker sentiment across financial markets as drivers of Bitcoin's decline.

Options traders have turned increasingly bearish. Over the past week, 1.7 put options, which pay out when prices fall, changed hands for every call on a seven-day average, the most since June 2022, Glassnode said in its weekly report. Measured by open interest, the ratio is at its highest since May 2021.

Bitcoin is back at its summer lows near $60K, and stocks are also in a downtrend.

BTC gave back the whole NVIDIA rally in less than six hours, an indication of severe relative weakness.

More on capitulation and leverage in this week's Week On-chain. https://t.co/GwEUc1pqHW

— glassnode (@glassnode) November 24, 2026

Such readings do not always mark a bottom. In June 2022, a similar reading coincided with a price low, but the bear market's final low was still five months away, while the open interest peak in April 2021 came near a market top, Glassnode noted.

Glassnode also said options dealers are "short gamma" between $58,000 and $64,000, meaning their hedging requires them to sell as prices fall and buy as they rise, which can make moves in either direction larger. Just outside that range, their hedging would slow a move, the firm said.

Glassnode's report found that Bitcoin investors are locking in their heaviest losses since the collapse of FTX.

A clearer outlook on interest rates and renewed ETF inflows could help bring stability back to the market, Andersson said.

#4877. The 8 Best Resistance Bands to Pack in Your Gym Bag, According to Fitness Experts

These bands can make a big difference in your workouts.

Our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved. We may earn a commission through links on our site. Why Trust Us?

IF YOU WANT to gain muscle, your first instinct may be to head to the gym and hit the dumbbells. And while lifting will never go out of style (in our humble opinion), we're here to tell you that's not the only way to build strength. If you're short on gear—or even just want to shake things up—it's time to add some of the best resistance bands to your training arsenal.

Resistance bands are relatively affordable, lightweight, and compact. Most importantly, they're one of the most versatile strength accessories you can buy. Adding a resistance band into your routine can be as simple as integrating it into your bodyweight warmup, or looping it onto a kettlebell to add a little extra heat to a set of swings.

"Because of the elastic properties, resistance bands recruit muscle fibers differently than free weights," explains Juan Guadarrama, CSCS, one of the creators of Men’s Health’s "7-Minute Workouts for Fat Burn".

Of course, there are tons of different types of resistance bands (and resistance band exercises) out there, from closed loop bands, thick latex bands, and bands with handles to ones that use anchors to attach to your door. Depending on the thickness, they also provide different levels of resistance, meaning that not every band workout is for light weights.

We've spent years testing dozens of the best exercise bands of nearly every type and thickness. Men's Health fitness editors, in collaboration with Men's Health Strength in Diversity initiative members Guadarrama and Eric Sung, CSCS (a trainer at Performance Lab in New York City) have compared testing notes on the best resistance bands we've tried to break down what factors set the best apart from the rest.

REP Fitness’s looped bands are durable, affordable, and have a wide weight range. With resistance profiles starting as low as five pounds (3X-Light) and as high as 150 (X-Heavy), users can gradually progress any exercise over time. They’re built with layered elastic and smoothed edges to create a smoother feel as the bands stretch and to reduce the chance of fraying (which can lead to breakage). The bands are color-coded and have the weight ranges printed clearly on each band, so I instantly know what I’m grabbing.

Marketed primarily as pull-up bands, their 38-inch length makes sense for assisted bodyweight work. However, for other moves—like curls or RDLs—that length can feel unwieldy. Still, with small adjustments, such as gripping lower on the band, double-looping the band, or widening your stance to take up slack, they function just great across a wide range of exercises.

The best value comes from REP’s five-band set (2X-Light through Heavy) at $70; it’s $50 cheaper than buying each band individually. Each band includes a one-year home-use warranty (and six months for commercial use).

Read More: The Best Items For Your Gym Bag

Leekey’s bands cover most bases for most folks. If you’re looking for a middle-of-the-road set of looped bands to pack in your bag for travel workouts or to help with assisted pull-ups, dips, and push-ups, this is a solid choice for under $40. The brand offers many options, so carefully review the choices before selecting. With multiple bundle options available, I think the best value is one of the five-band sets with the included door anchor.

Because Leekey isn’t completely transparent about the build quality, proceed with caution before pulling these toward your face or looping them over barbells for heavy pulls. A small percentage of reviewers reported snapping, though it’s unclear whether they overstretched the bands. Still, the product holds a 4.6-star average across more than 11,500 reviews. One customer even posted a photo of the purple bands draped over a barbell loaded with 405 pounds, writing: “I have been using these bands for added resistance on deadlifts and rack pulls. They are holding up well and help with adding resistance at the lockout of the pull.”

Read More: The Best Resistance Band Workouts

This set earns a spot for the sheer amount of resistance it offers—up to 300 pounds, more than any other kit on our list. That’s more than enough tension to challenge even advanced lifters. HPYGN also sells lighter-weight bundles at lower prices, but every option comes with the basics: a travel pouch, door anchor, handles, and ankle/wrist straps.

With over 10,000 reviews and a 4.5-star average, it’s an Amazon favorite. Some users note that bands have snapped under strain or that the listed resistance feels exaggerated, though the latter is subjective. On the flip side, many reviewers praise the sturdier build. One wrote: “I was pleasantly surprised that the gear looked like the ads and worked well. I bought it because of the metal carabiners that make it easy to change bands, and I wasn’t disappointed.”

You’ll need a solid anchor point to get the most out of these, and long-term durability is a question mark. Still, if you’re trying to ditch your gym membership or want a heavy-duty band system for travel, HPYGN’s kit is a worthy pick. It’s affordable, versatile, and capable of potentially replacing machines and free weights.

This rig gives you a little more than just the bands. We put this setup to the test, and found it to be super fun and intuitive to use. You can think of the Gorilla Bow as a hybrid tool that combines the benefits of resistance bands with a bow-style bar, which allows for a lot more versatility than a resistance band alone.

The unique bow design accommodates up to 300 pounds of resistance (just to start, you can get heavier models) that you can use to target just about every muscle group. The bow itself is made out of aircraft aluminum while the resistance bands are double-wall latex, resulting in a durable, lightweight, and portable build.

Resistance is adjustable, with the bow supporting up to four bands at a time so you can customize your resistance to meet your needs. The set comes with one original 56-inch bow, four Gorilla Bands (10, 20, 30 and 50-pounds), a band wrap, and a 30-day all-access membership to Gorilla Bow's virtual training platform. It's pricey, yes. But it packs a lot more usability than your average standalone resistance band.

Mini bands are a staple for warm-ups and recovery work, often wrapped around the knees for lateral walks or used to cue better glute and abductor activation during squats. Titan’s version is a little different. Designed initially as attachments for the brand’s Vice Grip Trainer, these bands double as standalone mini bands. And because they’re built for machine resistance, they’re thicker, more durable, and provide far greater tension than typical minis.

The resistance ranges from 15 pounds up to 120 pounds, which means the lightest bands are great for activation drills, while the heavy green band can push your lateral walks well past warm-up territory.

The catch is price. At nearly $50, these cost significantly more than most mini-band sets, and their uses are inherently limited compared to looped or tube bands. Still, the build quality is excellent, and the extra resistance opens the door for more challenging work than you’ll get with cheaper, flimsier bands. If you’re willing to invest once for a set that won’t wear out quickly, Titan’s mini bands are a “buy once, cry once” purchase.

Rogue is synonymous with quality in the fitness equipment space, and its tube resistance bands live up to the reputation. If you’re looking for bands to actually build workouts around—not just warm up with—these are among the best. The textured rubber handles stand out: they’re coated in a knurl-like pattern that gives you a secure grip, even when your hands get sweaty.

I noted that REP Fitness’s loop bands were long at 38 inches, and Rogue’s bands clock even longer at an elastic length of 48 inches. However, the length does allow you to perform overhead presses, lateral raises, and kickbacks with the bands. To increase the tension, loop the band around a squat rack or pole and take a few steps back. (Though Rogue warns users not to overstretch the band.) Each band is a standalone product, so you can’t clip multiple elastic tubes to a pair of handles, as with other models.

Price-wise, individual bands cost a bit more than some competitors, but Rogue makes up for it with bundle pricing. A light set (bands 0-2) runs $36.50, the heavy set (3-5) is $45, and the full collection is $75. Considering the quality and the savings versus buying separately, the sets are where the real value lies. For those who want tube bands tough enough for serious training, Rogue delivers.

These resistance bands feature four tubes braided together to create a durable workout tool that can stand up to your toughest sessions. We love that users can choose from five resistance levels, ranging from feather-light to heavy-duty, and select the perfect size and tension based on their preferences and fitness level. We found the handles comfortable, featuring a protective sleeve and grommet reinforcement which helps to ensure a solid grip.

While they excel in mobility work, don't expect crazy heavy resistance. They come in five resistance levels, from 'very light' to 'very heavy', ranging from 3 to 27 pounds. The various levels also differ in length, ranging from the 44-inch very light cord to the very heavy 53-inch cord, so you can pick the size and tension right for you.

If you want to go all in with resistance bands, WHATAFIT offers five bands (10, 20, 30, 40, 50-pound listed resistances), handles, ankle straps, a door anchor, and a carrying pouch. Some bundles even come with additional looped or mini bands. You’re not going to get much closer to having a complete gym in your home—especially for under $40—than with this set.

The set is also wildly popular: With a 4.6-star average and over 34,000 reviews—more than any other band on this list—it has the people’s approval. You can stack the bands for more precise resistance, which makes progressive overload easier and mimics the flexibility you’d get in a commercial gym. As one reviewer put it: “The materials feel high-quality and durable, and the bands have held up really well so far. I’ve used them for upper body, lower body, and core training without any issues. Plus, the whole set is compact and easy to store or travel with.”

What holds it back slightly is that these bands are serviceable, not premium. While natural latex is great for elasticity, it can degrade over time with sweat, sun, and repeated stretch cycles, so expect some wear. That said, for the price, this set offers a wide breadth of use and works well for someone building up strength or who needs a versatile “one-stop” band kit.

Your most important consideration should be how you plan to use your resistance bands—for solo workouts, to add resistance to exercises, to help you with dips or pull-ups, or to warm up before your lifts. No one band will perfectly check every box.

Most resistance bands are made from latex and rubber (or some combination of the two) and use plastic parts for accessories like handles and door anchors. (If you have a latex allergy, there are latex-free resistance bands.) So we’re not going to list materials as a significant consideration.

Likewise, the bands in this guide are all similar in price, with no major outliers. Premium and/or unique band designs cost more, but expect to pay between $20 and $70 for bands. The price scales based on the band resistance and whether or not you’re buying a set. Below are the top three things you should consider when shopping around for a new resistance band.

The type of band you buy dictates the kind of workouts you can perform. Here’s a quick breakdown of the band styles you’ll see, save for a few unique models, most of which are on this list.

Also referred to as super bands, these are the quintessential resistance bands that most manufacturers sell. Because the band is a single loop, you have to get creative in performing specific exercises, but you can target most major muscles with a looped band. You can also wrap them around pull-up bars, barbells, and machines to change the resistance profile of an exercise.

Popular in physical therapy offices, mini bands are an excellent tool for activating the smaller muscles in your hips, legs, upper back, and shoulders. They can’t support your bodyweight and they don’t stretch far enough to allow for squats, presses, or curls. Think of these as a warm-up tool, not a workout replacement.

These bands are defined by a single tube of rubber with a handle on each end (usually). These bands give you the most freedom of movement, and the handles allow you to press and row more efficiently (compared to looped bands).

Some bands cite a single poundage versus a range. If a band lists its resistance as between 20 and 60 force, you’ll experience 20 pounds of resistance when the band is least stretched and 60 pounds at the most stretched position. Squatting with a 50-pound band doesn’t feel the same as squatting with a 50-pound dumbbell, either, since the force you’re resisting is literally changing with every inch you move.

To track your progress effectively, find a band that has you reaching within one to three reps of failure for your desired rep range. Stick with that band until the reps feel easier, and then move up to the next heaviest band you have. Progressing with bands isn’t as easy as with free weights and machines, but you'll make gains as long as you’re basing your effort on training intensity and not weight.

Resistance bands can be dangerous. If they snap while doing assisted pull-ups or a face pull, you’ll fall or injure your eyes or face. No band is wear-proof, so it’s essential to use them responsibly: don’t overstretch, inspect them regularly for tears, and avoid anchoring them against textured surfaces like the knurling on a barbell, which creates friction that weakens the material.

Manufacturers use different strategies to improve longevity. Some bands are built from layered latex for added reinforcement, while others encase the elastic in a protective sleeve that reduces wear and shields the user from a whip-like snap mid-rep. These features can’t eliminate risk, but they can extend the lifespan of your bands and make training safer.

As a longtime fitness journalist and NASM-certified trainer, I have spent years using resistance bands in a variety of exercise scenarios. For this story, I worked in tandem with the team at Men's Health, including Fitness Director Ebenezer Samuel, CSCS, and Fitness and Commerce Editor Charles Thorp, NASM. We also recruited the help of MH Strength in Diversity members Juan Guadarrama, CSCS and Eric Sung, CSCS to gather diverse perspectives on the topic.

We used our collective experience to put together a testing pool by putting the most popular designs that we could put up against new offerings from classic brands as well as newcomers to the market. Both historically and in the pursuit of this story, we used these designs during band-only workouts, athletic movements, and to advance fundamental movements like the deadlift. The selections above represent the best resistance bands that you can buy now.

We asked Strength in Diversity member Eric Sung about his favorite ways to incorporate resistance bands with clients and in his own training.

"The banded rear delt fly is great exercise to do as a warm up to prepare your body before an upper body session," says Sung. "Grab the band, hold it out in front of you, stretch it across your upper chest and try to resist the band as much and slowly as you can."

If you're looking to get started in training lower body plyometrics, put band-assisted squat jumps on your radar. "Tie a band to a high anchor, grab each end of it, assume your squat stance, and focus on jumping as high as you can with the assistance of the band. This is a great entry point," he adds.

For more ideas, check out our list of 12 resistance band workouts you can do at home.

Similar to free weights, resistance bands help create tension and place stress on the muscles, explains Sung. However, resistance bands assist in efforts to build muscle and strength in a few unique ways.

Because they deliver more resistance as you stretch them further, they offer a different challenge than free weights. This means your muscles face the most load and tension at the top of every exercise. For example, the top of a resistance band pushup is a challenge; the top of a bodyweight pushup is a position of rest.

Another way resistance bands help build strength is by assisting in movements that an individual cannot yet complete at baseline standards, explains Guadarrama. "It allows athletes to move through the full range of motion and acquire neuromuscular capacity," he explains. "Over time the body can adapt, learn the movement, and build the strength needed for the unassisted effort."

Bands can also be attached to plates and kettlebells to add more resistance to the eccentric or concentric phases of a given movement, explains Guadarrama. "Each of these methods has benefits to biomechanical advantages and providing variance in stress," he says.

Andrew Gutman, NASM-CPT is a journalist with a decade of experience covering fitness and nutrition. His work has been published in Men's Health, Men's Journal, Muscle & Fitness, and Gear Patrol.
